teaching_blocks.title: Mission and Values in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a company whose stated mission is to help small shop owners manage daily orders. Its values include clarity and respect for customers' time. You are asked whether an entertaining social feed belongs in its product. The first question is not whether the idea sounds exciting, but whether it fits that purpose and those principles.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A mission states the present purpose of an organization and whom it serves. Values express the principles that guide how an organization pursues its purpose.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: A product direction should fit the organization’s mission and values. Check a proposed product direction against the organization’s stated purpose.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For this invented company, compare two proposals. A clear list of outstanding orders directly helps shop owners manage their day. A social feed devoted to unrelated celebrity news does not have an evident connection to that purpose. You could explain the first proposal as consistent with the mission, while asking the proposer of the second to establish a relevant connection before endorsing it. Now consider a confusing order screen filled with promotional interruptions. Even though the screen concerns orders, the interruptions conflict with the example company's commitment to clarity and respect for customers' time.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Treat purpose and principles as two questions applied to the same decision: whom does this serve, and is the proposed behavior consistent with how the organization says it will serve them? In this example, mentioning orders is not enough to demonstrate alignment with both. Your judgment should point to the actual words in the mission and values and the actual behavior of the proposal, rather than simply calling an idea a good fit.

video_need.reason: The purpose-and-principles filter is understandable from the two feature comparisons; a simple written comparison suffices.

teaching_blocks.title: Product Vision Statement in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The same shop-order team wants a shared picture of the future it is trying to create. One person imagines shop owners confidently finishing the day; another talks only about adding three screens. Those are different kinds of statements. A product vision gives the team a future to work toward, rather than substituting a task list for direction.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Product vision describes the future state a product is intended to achieve and the value it will provide. Vision gives a shared direction for decisions rather than a list of detailed implementation tasks.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Draft a vision by stating the product’s purpose, the customers it serves, and the desired future impact. Review a draft vision with the team and target users to refine whether it is clear and motivating.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: An illustrative draft is: “Help small shop owners finish every day confident that their orders are accounted for.” It names the audience and a desired future impact. Compare it with “Add an orders screen, a search box, and two buttons.” The second draft describes implementation tasks, but does not explain the future value those tasks are meant to provide. Bring the first draft to the team and target shop owners. Ask what they understand by “accounted for” and whether the statement describes a future that matters to them. Their responses would give you material for refining the wording, not evidence that the future has already been achieved.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Read a draft from the customer's point of view first, then from the team's. Can the customer recognize the intended value? Can the team identify a shared direction without treating the wording as detailed instructions? If “accounted for” proves unclear, a revised statement might emphasize knowing which orders remain unfinished. Keep the distinction between refining the direction and rewriting it whenever a small implementation detail changes.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A vision should not be rewritten for every small change in the product’s underlying plan.

teaching_blocks.title: Value Proposition in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A shop owner hears that your product has filters, labels, and an order list, but still asks, “What does that do for me?” Naming capabilities has not yet communicated value. The work here is to connect a specific customer's problem to a benefit they can understand, rather than expecting the customer to infer it from feature names.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A value proposition communicates the benefit a product delivers to a specific target customer. The message should address the customer’s problem or job and explain the benefit or gain the product creates.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write a proposition by naming the target customer, the problem relieved, and the distinct benefit provided. Check that the value is expressed in terms the customer can understand rather than a list of product features.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the target customers are small shop owners who lose track of unfinished orders among paper notes. An illustrative proposition is: “For small shop owners managing orders on paper, our shared order list helps you see what still needs attention without searching through scattered notes.” The customer, problem, and benefit are all visible. The phrase “shared order list” identifies the proposed product capability, but the sentence does not stop there: it explains the customer's gain. Compare “Advanced filtering and color-coded status labels.” That might describe the product, yet it leaves this customer's problem and benefit unstated. In this example, the distinctive benefit you want to communicate is a single understandable view of unfinished work.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Check the sentence by separating who it serves, what difficulty it addresses, and what benefit it offers. If one part is missing, rewrite that part rather than adding more feature adjectives. A proposition for this shop-owner segment need not claim to help every possible customer. Keep hypothetical benefit wording separate from an unsupported promise that the product has already produced a measured result.

teaching_blocks.title: Competitive Analysis in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A shop owner considering your order product could instead use another app, a spreadsheet, or paper. Looking only at products that resemble yours would leave some customer choices out of the comparison. Competitive analysis starts with alternatives the customer could actually choose and examines them on shared dimensions.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Competitive analysis examines alternatives customers could choose, including indirect competitors. A structured comparison can include features, pricing, market position, strengths, and weaknesses.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Identify the relevant competitors and compare them using the same dimensions. Use gaps, weaknesses, and differences in the comparison to identify an opportunity or threat relevant to the product.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Create an illustrative comparison of three alternatives: an order app, a spreadsheet, and paper notes. Use the same headings for each, such as price, how unfinished orders are shown, and the kind of customer each serves. Suppose your example observations say the app has a shared status view at a monthly price, the spreadsheet is familiar but needs manual setup, and paper notes have no shared status view. These are invented comparison inputs, not claims about real products. A possible opportunity is to provide a simple shared view for owners who find spreadsheet setup difficult. A possible threat is that the existing app already serves this need well. The comparison supports asking those questions; it does not guarantee success.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Keep the dimensions stable as you move between alternatives. Comparing one competitor's price with another competitor's ease of use does not yet show their differences on either dimension. Describe the relevant gap and connect it to your product decision: which customer problem could it help address, or which alternative could make your proposal less compelling? Include indirect alternatives without pretending every alternative has identical capabilities.

teaching_blocks.title: Strategic Positioning in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Two products may help with orders but be presented very differently: one for large operations, another for owners who need a simple daily view. Positioning concerns the intended market and the product's relationship to alternatives. The question is not merely what the product contains, but how its customer benefit and difference are expressed.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Product positioning describes how a product is presented to its intended market relative to alternatives.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: A positioning statement typically identifies who the product is for, what problem it solves, what category it competes in, and what makes it different. Write positioning by completing those elements and checking whether it emphasizes customer benefits instead of merely listing features.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented shop-order product, draft: “For small shop owners who lose track of unfinished orders, our order-management tool provides a clear daily view, unlike scattered paper notes that require checking several places.” The statement identifies the audience, problem, category, and intended difference. Its comparison is limited to the example's paper-note alternative; it does not claim superiority over every product in the market. Compare this with “Our product has labels and a search box.” That sentence omits the intended market and relationship to alternatives. If your earlier comparison indicates that another tool already offers a clear daily view, revisit whether the claimed difference is meaningful in that competitive set.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: A useful review separates the statement's elements and checks whether they add up to a customer benefit. Being in a category is not itself the same as being different within it. Keep “typically” in mind: the elements are a useful drafting pattern, not a claim that every positioning statement must have identical wording. If the market changes, reconsider the message rather than treating this first draft as permanently correct.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Positioning is not a fixed message that should remain unchanged when the market changes.

teaching_blocks.title: Business Goals Alignment in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A team says, “We will add a reminder feature this quarter.” The organization says, “We need customers to keep using the service.” One statement describes work; the other describes a desired benefit. Alignment requires explaining how the proposed work supports a measurable outcome, rather than assuming that completing it proves progress toward the business goal.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Product goals describe outcomes the product should achieve, not just activities a team will carry out. Business goals describe the benefit the product should deliver to the organization.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Connect product initiatives to measurable goals that support the organization’s direction. Specify a goal’s intended result, measurement, and time boundary so progress can be assessed.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose an invented business goal is to improve continued use among small-shop customers over the next quarter. A corresponding product goal could be to raise the proportion of those customers completing their weekly order review from 40% to 50% during that period. A reminder proposal has a plausible intended link: it is meant to help customers return to unfinished order work. State that link as an expectation, not an established cause. A proposal that increases distracting promotional interactions could create local activity while conflicting with the broader direction of helping customers manage orders. Both proposals might generate completed tasks for the team, yet their relationship to the stated outcome differs.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Trace the chain in plain language: proposed initiative, intended product result, and organizational benefit. Then name how the result will be measured and when it will be assessed. In this example, “finish the reminder” is an activity milestone; “increase weekly review completion by quarter end” is an outcome target. If you cannot explain the connection, ask for clarification or reject the claimed alignment instead of treating any measurable activity as the business goal.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A product decision can create local progress while conflicting with a higher-level strategy.

teaching_blocks.title: Customer Interviews in product work
teaching_blocks.content: You want to understand why shop owners sometimes finish the day unsure which orders remain open. Asking “Would our reminder solve this?” steers the conversation toward your proposal. An interview instead gives you room to hear the person's experience of the problem, including details your initial idea may have missed.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Customer interviews gather qualitative accounts of needs, experiences, and problems through guided conversation. Start an interview plan with a research goal and recruit people whose experience is relevant to it.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Build a discussion guide with open-ended, neutral prompts about concrete past experiences. During the conversation, listen and ask follow-up questions to clarify what happened, why it mattered, and how the person responded.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Set the research goal as understanding how owners check unfinished orders at closing time, and recruit people who have recently done that work. Your guide might begin, “Tell me about the last time you checked orders before closing.” Follow with “What did you look at first?”, “What happened next?”, and “What made that difficult?” If someone says they checked three notebooks, ask them to describe what they were looking for and how they decided they had finished. These prompts explore a concrete past experience without supplying the preferred answer. Record the account as what the participant reported, including the problem and its consequence, rather than converting it directly into proof of interface behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: The research goal keeps the conversation relevant; neutral prompts leave the answer open; follow-ups clarify meaning and context. A statement such as “It was confusing” becomes more useful when you understand what happened and why it mattered to that person. Keep the distinction between reported experience and directly observed behavior: this conversation can explain what someone says about using a screen, but it does not itself show them using it.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: An interview reports what a person says; it does not directly establish what they do while using an interface.

teaching_blocks.title: Jobs-to-Be-Done Framework in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A shop owner asks for a red notification badge. That is a feature request, but you still need to understand the outcome behind it. Perhaps the owner wants to leave work knowing that no paid order has been forgotten. Jobs to Be Done shifts attention from the requested interface element to the task or problem the customer is trying to resolve.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Jobs to Be Done examines the outcome a customer wants to achieve rather than starting from a feature. A customer job is a task or problem the person is trying to resolve, with functional, emotional, or social dimensions.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Identify a job by investigating the customer’s situation, obstacles, desired outcome, and existing way of getting the task done. Frame an opportunity around the desired outcome and compare current alternatives by how well they help achieve it. Write the job as a sentence describing what the customer needs to accomplish, the relevant situation and why they do it, and what counts as a successful outcome rather than naming a requested feature.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: In this invented scenario, investigate when the owner checks orders, what gets in the way, what a successful finish looks like, and how paper notes currently help or fail to help. A job statement might be: “When I close the shop, I need to identify every unfinished paid order so I can plan tomorrow's work and leave confident that nothing has been missed.” The task is identifying unfinished orders; the situation is closing time; the desired outcome includes both a plan and confidence. A badge is one possible response, not the job itself. You could compare paper notes and the proposed product by how well each supports that outcome, rather than by whether each contains the requested badge.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Look for functional, emotional, or social dimensions where the scenario supports them. Here, planning tomorrow's work is functional and leaving with confidence is emotional; there is no need to invent a social dimension just to fill a template. A clear job statement makes the desired accomplishment visible without selecting the feature in advance. Check that it still makes sense if the badge is removed from the sentence.

teaching_blocks.title: Voice of Customer in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Three customers ask for different changes: bigger status labels, clearer order names, and a better way to see unfinished work. Treating each request as a separate instruction could hide a recurring problem. Voice of Customer work collects feedback and looks for shared needs and consequences across the raw comments.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Voice of Customer captures feedback about customers’ experiences, needs, and preferences. Feedback can come from interviews, surveys, reviews, and customer-facing teams.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Collect feedback across channels and look for recurring needs and pain points rather than treating each request as a separate instruction. Use the recurring themes to identify opportunities that address customer problems. Group related observations into themes and record recurrence and the user consequence associated with each theme.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose your invented feedback set contains six comments about not recognizing order status and two about difficulty searching older orders. Group related observations under themes such as “unclear current status” and “finding past orders.” For each theme, retain the source observations, recurrence, and user consequence. In this example, the status theme appears six times and has caused owners to overlook unfinished work; the search theme appears twice and has cost time locating old records. Rank them with both recurrence and consequence visible, rather than reporting only a count. Include relevant interview, survey, review, and customer-facing-team feedback when available; the theme list should not silently stand for perspectives you never collected.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Move from comments to problems before moving from problems to opportunities. “Make the label bigger” is a proposed change; “I could not tell which orders were unfinished” expresses the underlying pain point. Related requests may belong to the same theme even when they suggest different solutions. The example ranking concerns the supplied feedback set, not a claim about how common those problems are among all customers.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A single feedback channel may omit important customer perspectives.

teaching_blocks.title: Survey Design in product work
teaching_blocks.content: You want to learn how often shop owners struggle to identify unfinished orders. A question such as “How easy and fast is our excellent order screen?” combines issues and suggests a favorable answer. Survey design begins with the information needed for the research question, then turns it into clear questions people can answer as intended.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Survey design starts with the research question and the information needed to answer it. Closed-ended questions provide predefined response options for quantitative summaries.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Open-ended questions allow respondents to describe their answer in their own words. Write questions in neutral, clear language and choose response options that are mutually exclusive and collectively cover plausible answers. Pilot a survey before distributing it to check whether people interpret the questions and options as intended. Ask about one issue per question so a respondent is not forced to give a single answer to two different questions.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative survey, ask “During the past seven days, on how many days did you check unfinished orders?” Offer 0, 1–2, 3–4, and 5–7 days. These ranges do not overlap and cover the possible counts in that period. A separate open-ended item could ask, “Describe a difficulty you encountered when checking unfinished orders, if any.” The first item supports a quantitative summary; the second lets people use their own words. If you need to ask about speed and clarity, use separate questions rather than forcing one answer to represent both. Pilot the draft with relevant respondents and ask how they interpreted the questions and options before distributing it more widely.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Review the question and response options together. Neutral wording is not enough if someone with a plausible answer cannot find a matching option. Conversely, a complete set of options does not rescue a leading question. This survey concerns reported recent experience. Asking “Will you use this every day next year?” would collect predictions, which are unreliable evidence of what respondents will actually do.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Respondents’ predictions of their future behavior are unreliable evidence of what they will actually do.

teaching_blocks.title: Market Segmentation in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Not every shop owner manages orders in the same way. Some work alone with a small daily list; others coordinate several workers across shifts. If research shows different needs and behaviors, a product direction aimed at one group may not describe the other well. Segmentation makes the intended user group more explicit.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: User groups can be distinguished by shared behaviors, goals, needs, and pain points. Segments help specify which users a product direction is intended to serve.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Derive useful groups by looking for recurring similarities and differences in research about user behavior and needs. Define a proposed segment’s common need and relevant characteristics, then check it against the intended audience and product direction.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose research in your example distinguishes owners who personally check every order from owners who rely on staff handoffs. The first group needs a quick personal overview; the second repeatedly needs shared visibility across workers. Define a proposed segment as “shops coordinating unfinished orders across shifts,” and record the relevant shared need and behavior. Then check whether that group matches the intended audience and product direction. Compare this with grouping owners only by age. Two similarly aged owners in the example could work very differently, while owners of different ages could share the same handoff problem. The useful distinction here comes from research about how the work happens.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Look for recurring similarities within a group and meaningful differences between groups. A segment is not just a label attached to one memorable participant. Explain its common need in enough detail that a reader can see why your proposed product direction serves it. Demographic information may be part of the description, but demographic similarity alone need not establish common goals or behaviors.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Demographic similarity alone need not imply similar user goals or behaviors.

teaching_blocks.title: Market Sizing (TAM/SAM/SOM) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Someone says the market is worth millions, but the team does not know which customers the figure includes or what revenue it assumes. Market sizing turns that broad claim into estimates with visible boundaries. Keep the total opportunity, the geographically reachable portion, and the realistically obtainable portion distinct.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Total Addressable Market estimates the total potential market opportunity for a product or service. A top-down estimate narrows a broad market using external industry data and relevant constraints.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: A bottom-up estimate uses the number of potential customers and annual revenue per customer to estimate annual market revenue. Document the customer-count and revenue assumptions and, for the obtainable market, the time horizon and assumptions about willingness to buy, marketing and distribution reach, and competition. The Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM) is the portion of TAM within geographical reach; estimate its annual revenue by multiplying the reachable potential-customer count by annual revenue per customer. The Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM) is the portion of SAM realistically achievable; calculate it as SAM multiplied by an assumed achievable share for the chosen period, treating that share as an estimate rather than guaranteed demand.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Use invented annual figures. Suppose 10,000 potential shops could each generate $120 per year. A bottom-up TAM estimate is 10,000 × $120 = $1,200,000 in annual market revenue. If 4,000 of those shops are within geographical reach, SAM is 4,000 × $120 = $480,000 annually. If you assume the business could achieve 5% of that SAM within a chosen one-year horizon, SOM is $480,000 × 0.05 = $24,000 annually. This corresponds to 200 shops under the same revenue assumption. State why you assumed that share, including willingness to buy, reach through marketing and distribution, and competition. None of the multiplication establishes that those shops will actually purchase.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: A top-down estimate would instead begin with external industry data and narrow it using relevant constraints. In either approach, make the customer boundary and annual revenue assumptions visible so the reader knows what is being estimated. Do not mix monthly revenue per customer with an annual market total. teaching_blocks.title: Persona Development in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team remembers one particularly persuasive interview participant, but needs a representation of a recurring user type rather than a biography of that individual. A persona consolidates research patterns so a product decision can be examined against relevant goals, behavior, motivations, and pain points.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A user persona represents a recurring type of user grounded in research about needs and behavior. A persona should communicate relevant goals, behaviors, motivations, and pain points.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Draft a persona by consolidating research patterns and recording the user’s goal, activities, and problem context. Use the persona to examine whether a proposed product decision addresses that user type’s needs.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose several researched shop owners personally check unfinished orders at closing time and worry about missing paid work. Draft a persona describing the goal of leaving with a reliable next-day plan, the activity of checking orders, and the pain point of reconciling scattered notes. You may give this illustrative persona a name, such as Sam, to make discussion easier, but the name does not supply evidence. When someone proposes an order-summary view, ask whether it addresses this recurring user's closing-time need. When someone proposes an unrelated news feed, identify the missing connection instead of saying that “Sam would probably love it.” The relevant persona content is the research-grounded work and problem context.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Separate the patterns from decorative details. A photograph or plausible backstory cannot repair missing research about the user's needs. Nor does one persona need to represent every segment the product could serve. In this example, the decision is checked against a user type that personally reviews orders; a team coordinating shift handoffs may require a different representation grounded in its own recurring behaviors.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Adding a plausible name or photograph does not replace research into user needs.

teaching_blocks.title: Usability Testing (Running Sessions) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A customer says an order screen looks simple, yet you do not know whether they can find unfinished work on it. A usability session addresses that gap by observing a representative user attempting a realistic task. The useful evidence is where they succeed or struggle, not just whether they say they like the design.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A usability test observes representative users attempting tasks with a product or prototype. A basic usability test involves a participant, task, and facilitator.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Select realistic tasks and participants relevant to the product’s intended use. Observe where participants succeed or struggle and record the evidence without directing them toward the answer. Summarize observed obstacles into findings that can guide improvements.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Choose a participant who actually manages shop orders. Give a task such as “Find which paid orders still need to be completed before closing,” using an illustrative product or prototype. Do not say “Click the blue status button,” because that supplies a route instead of leaving the task attempt observable. As facilitator, record actions and obstacles: perhaps the participant searches completed orders first, overlooks the status label, then finds the right list. Capture what occurred without turning your interpretation into an observed fact. Summarize the obstacle as difficulty recognizing the route to unfinished orders, supported by the recorded actions. The session may guide an improvement, but a positive opinion about the screen would not replace this task evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Keep participant, task, and facilitator roles clear. Your job in the example is to make the intended task available and observe the attempt, not to demonstrate the correct steps whenever the participant hesitates. A finding should link back to what happened during the task. That makes “the participant selected the completed-order view first” more useful than the unsupported conclusion “all users dislike this screen.”

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Usability testing is not the same as asking people whether they like an interface.

teaching_blocks.title: Product-Market Fit in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A shop-order product receives an enthusiastic compliment and a burst of signups. The team wants to declare product-market fit immediately. Those signals are worth examining, but fit concerns a significant need and customers' willingness to use or pay for the product, not one encouraging moment in isolation.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Product-market fit means a product meets a significant market need and customers are willing to use or pay for it. Qualitative customer feedback and quantitative indicators can contribute evidence of product-market fit.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Gather evidence of demand and customer value from willingness to pay, satisfaction, and recommendations. Assess fit from a combination of evidence rather than declaring it from one isolated response. A retention curve that declines initially and then stabilizes at a healthy level supports a judgment of product-market fit, while a curve declining toward zero signals problems with delivered value or onboarding. Distinguish early from sustained retention when judging fit: early retention can reflect onboarding, whereas later retention shows lasting usage habits, and the curve alone does not explain why users leave. Customer word of mouth supports demand-driven growth, but an increase in signups can arise from external publicity rather than from customer recommendations.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Consider invented evidence from one customer group. Some owners recommend the product, several describe a meaningful improvement in their order work, and others are willing to pay. A retention chart falls after initial use and then stabilizes at a level judged healthy for this product. Together, those observations support a fit judgment more than one compliment would. Now compare a second scenario: signups rise after a news story, but continued usage declines toward zero. The signup increase could reflect external publicity rather than customer recommendations, while the retention decline signals possible value or onboarding problems. The curve alone does not identify which explanation is correct. Ask what other qualitative and quantitative evidence bears on the judgment.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Separate early from sustained retention. Early departures can reflect onboarding, while later retention shows lasting usage habits. Do not assign a universal numerical threshold for a healthy level when the supplied evidence gives none. Likewise, treat willingness to pay, satisfaction, and recommendations as contributing evidence rather than interchangeable proofs. The task is to assess the combination and describe its limits, not to select the most flattering isolated number.

teaching_blocks.title: Problem Statement in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A request arrives saying, “We need a reminder button.” Before specifying that feature, identify the user difficulty that makes the request matter. A problem statement should remain understandable even if the team ultimately chooses a different solution. It names the affected user, what happens, and the consequence supported by evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A problem statement identifies the affected user, the problem, and its consequence without prescribing a solution. Evidence of the problem should connect it to an observable cost such as wasted time, money, or dissatisfaction.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write a problem statement by naming who encounters the problem, what happens, and why it matters. Check that a draft focuses on the user problem rather than a favored feature.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose your illustrative research records show that shop owners spend 20 minutes at closing reconciling scattered order notes and sometimes miss unfinished paid orders. A draft could be: “Shop owners checking work at closing struggle to identify unfinished paid orders across scattered notes, costing time and leaving work overlooked.” The user, difficulty, and consequence are visible. Compare “Shop owners lack our reminder button.” That describes absence of a favored feature rather than the underlying problem. You could investigate a clearer summary or another approach without rewriting the first statement. Keep the numerical detail tied to the supplied example evidence, rather than presenting it as a general fact about all shops.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Underline the user, problem, and consequence in the draft. If the only problem you can underline is the missing feature, return to the evidence about the person's work. If the consequence is merely “bad experience,” clarify the observed cost such as time, money, or dissatisfaction. The goal is an evidence-backed difficulty, not a persuasive description of the solution you already prefer.

teaching_blocks.title: Problem Reframing and Ideation in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Your problem statement says owners struggle to identify unfinished orders at closing. The team immediately suggests a notification badge. Reframing gives the team a focused question that admits more than that first answer, while ideation creates alternatives before judging which one to pursue.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: How Might We questions turn research problems or insights into prompts for solution exploration. A useful prompt is broad enough to admit multiple approaches but specific enough to focus on the identified problem.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write a prompt as “How might we” followed by the desired user outcome, without naming a particular solution. Prefer positive outcome language that makes the desired change clear. Generate alternative ideas without judging them during the initial brainstorming phase.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: A useful illustrative prompt is “How might we help shop owners identify unfinished orders before closing?” It describes a positive desired outcome without naming an interface element. “How might we add a red badge?” already chooses a solution. “How might we improve everything about running a shop?” is too broad to focus this particular problem. With the outcome-focused prompt, initially list alternatives such as a closing summary, a clearer status view, or an order checklist. At this brainstorming stage, collect the alternatives without judging them as they are proposed. The exercise does not establish that any one idea works; it keeps solution exploration open around the research problem.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Check both sides of the prompt's boundary. It should be broad enough for genuinely different approaches, yet specific enough that an idea can be related to the identified difficulty. Positive outcome language helps make the intended change visible. If every answer must contain your preferred badge, the wording is probably still selecting the solution instead of opening exploration.

teaching_blocks.title: Solution Specification in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team has chosen to explore a closing-time order summary. “Make orders easier to manage” no longer gives design and engineering enough information about the proposed change. A solution specification explains its intended behavior and boundaries while retaining the connection to the user problem and goals.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A solution specification describes the proposed behavior and boundaries of the product change. The specification links the proposal to the user problem, goals, functional behavior, and constraints.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write the proposal by explaining the approach, expected behavior, included scope, exclusions, and key constraints. Review it with engineering and design to resolve ambiguity before implementation.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented proposal, state that the summary shows unfinished paid orders for the selected day and lets the owner open an order's details. Include that view and detail access in scope; exclude editing payment history and redesigning the whole order product. Explain the associated goal of making unfinished work visible at closing. Record a constraint such as using the existing order-status information, and identify unanswered behavior questions: what appears when there are no unfinished orders, and which day is initially shown? Review these points with engineering and design before implementation. The example is a proposal to be clarified, not a claim about how an existing tool behaves.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Read the specification as someone trying to understand both what changes and what does not. The expected behavior addresses “what happens”; scope and exclusions address “how far this proposal goes”; constraints explain boundaries it must respect. If different readers could implement substantially different behaviors from the same wording, bring those ambiguities into the review instead of treating a long document as automatically clear.

teaching_blocks.title: Problem/Solution Separation in product work
teaching_blocks.content: “Owners need a closing-summary screen because there is no closing-summary screen” sounds like a problem statement, but it defines the problem as absence of the proposed solution. Separating problem and proposal exposes what the team knows about the user difficulty and what it has chosen to do about it.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A problem statement describes the user need or difficulty; a solution statement describes a proposed way of addressing it. Combining the two too early can hide assumptions and narrow the alternatives the team considers.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Rewrite a muddled statement into a problem describing who is affected and why, followed by a separate proposal describing the chosen behavior. Check that the proposed solution addresses the stated problem without redefining the problem as the absence of that solution.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Rewrite the invented statement in two parts. Problem: “At closing, shop owners struggle to identify unfinished paid orders across scattered records, leaving work overlooked.” Proposal: “Provide a summary of unfinished paid orders with access to each order's details.” The first part states who is affected and why the difficulty matters. The second describes the chosen behavior. A different proposal could still address the same problem, which is precisely what was obscured by the original wording. Review whether this particular summary would help identify the unfinished work; do not quietly redefine the problem as a need for summaries simply because a summary is now the preferred approach.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Use the separation to inspect assumptions. The existence of a proposed screen does not demonstrate that it addresses the recorded difficulty. Likewise, a well-written problem does not uniquely determine a solution. Keeping the two statements readable on their own lets the team discuss the problem evidence and the proposed response without treating agreement with one as automatic agreement with the other.

teaching_blocks.title: Product Requirements Document (PRD) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: An engineer and designer agree that a closing summary is useful, but interpret its behavior differently. One expects a single day's orders; the other expects every unfinished order. A PRD organizes the product's purpose and requirements so these differences can be discussed before work proceeds under incompatible assumptions.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A product specification describes what is to be built and the requirements it must satisfy. A PRD captures a product’s purpose, features, behavior, and release requirements.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Construct a specification with purpose, user needs, functional and nonfunctional requirements, scope, and constraints. Review the specification with engineering and design to clarify ambiguity and missing requirements.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Draft an illustrative PRD with the purpose of helping owners identify unfinished work at closing, the user need behind it, and the proposed summary feature. Specify functional behavior such as showing unfinished paid orders and opening details. Record nonfunctional requirements and constraints explicitly when they are agreed; for example, a stipulated response-time requirement belongs in the document rather than being invented by an individual reader. Name included scope, exclusions, and release requirements. Ask engineering and design to examine ambiguous cases, such as the initial day selection and the empty state. If new information changes an agreed requirement, revise the specification instead of insisting that the first version remains authoritative regardless of what the team learns.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: A document is not clear merely because it contains headings. Readers need enough detail under those headings to understand what is to be built and what it must satisfy. Keep purpose and user needs connected to behavior, while leaving unknown requirements visible as questions for review. Do not fill a missing constraint with an unsupported technical claim just to make the PRD look complete.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A specification should evolve when new information changes the requirements; it is not necessarily a one-time handoff.

teaching_blocks.title: One-Pager in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A broad group needs to understand a closing-summary idea, but not every detail of the full specification. A one-page brief concentrates the problem, proposal, intended impact, and essential context. The challenge is to shorten the explanation without losing the purpose and boundaries that let the team discuss the idea meaningfully.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A product brief is a short document for aligning the team around an idea before detailed delivery work. Its core content is the problem, intended audience, goals, success metrics, scope, assumptions, and open questions.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Draft the brief by clarifying the problem and audience before describing the proposed approach. Share the brief for feedback and revise it until the team understands the purpose and boundaries of the work. For a requested one-page summary, keep the problem, proposed solution, intended impact, and essential context while removing specialist detail.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative one-pager, begin with shop owners' closing-time difficulty and the intended audience. Describe the proposed unfinished-order summary, the goal of making overlooked work visible, and the success measure the team intends to use. Name included scope and important exclusions. State assumptions, such as whether existing status information is sufficient, and open questions about which orders the view should include. Remove specialist detail that this audience does not need to understand the proposal, rather than removing the uncertainty itself. Share the brief and revise wording or boundaries where readers interpret them differently. The document is intended to align understanding before detailed delivery work, not to pretend all implementation questions have already been resolved.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Read the page as someone hearing about the idea for the first time. Can you identify the problem before the solution, the affected audience, and the intended impact? Can you tell what is outside the proposal? A page full of feature labels but missing the reason for the work is short without being a useful brief. Essential context matters more than preserving every specialist sentence.

teaching_blocks.title: User Stories in product work
teaching_blocks.content: “Build an orders endpoint” names work, but does not express the customer's desired outcome. A user story puts the person and reason back into the description. For a PM, the useful question is what capability the user wants and why it matters, not only which component someone might build.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A user story describes a desired outcome from a user’s perspective. The common story form is “As a [user], I want [capability], so that [benefit].”

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write a story by naming the user, the goal or capability, and the reason it matters. Discuss stories with the team and split large work into smaller stories that communicate distinct user value.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: An illustrative story is: “As a shop owner closing for the day, I want to see unfinished paid orders, so that I can plan the remaining work.” It names a user, a capability, and a benefit. If a proposed story also includes finding orders, editing payments, contacting customers, and preparing delivery routes, discuss it with the team and separate distinct user outcomes into smaller stories. For example, viewing unfinished orders and contacting the customer of a selected order could be separate stories when each communicates distinct value. The story wording supports that discussion; it does not supply every detailed technical or behavioral requirement needed to implement the work.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Check that the benefit explains the value of the capability for this user, rather than simply repeating the capability in different words. “So that I can see orders” adds little to “I want to see orders.” The common story form helps reveal missing elements, but its familiar shape should not tempt you to treat one sentence as a complete technical specification.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A user story is not a complete detailed technical specification.

teaching_blocks.title: Acceptance Criteria in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A team agrees to “make the closing summary work well,” but cannot tell whether the delivered behavior meets that requirement. Acceptance criteria turn the intended behavior of a particular work item into observable conditions. They give the team something concrete to compare with the delivery, rather than a vague impression of quality.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Acceptance criteria state the observable conditions a particular work item must satisfy to be accepted. Criteria should be clear and testable so the team can determine whether a condition is met.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write criteria around the intended behavior and relevant constraints rather than vague judgments. Use the criteria to compare the delivered behavior with the agreed requirements.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented summary story, agree that selecting a day shows that day's unfinished paid orders, completed orders do not appear in that result, and selecting an order opens its details. Add a condition for the no-results case if that behavior is part of the agreed requirement. Each criterion can be checked against a specific example: one unfinished paid order should appear; a completed order should not. “The screen is amazing” does not provide the same testable distinction. These conditions describe the required outcome. They need not dictate a particular internal storage method or component arrangement when those implementation choices are unnecessary to the requirement.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Read each criterion as a condition that could either be met or not met. If the team cannot describe what observation would distinguish those outcomes, clarify the wording. Then use the agreed conditions on the delivered behavior, not just on the original design proposal. Keep the criteria tied to this work item instead of turning them into a claim that every aspect of completion is covered by this one list.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Acceptance criteria should describe the required outcome without unnecessarily dictating its implementation.

teaching_blocks.title: User Flows in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A closing-summary screen exists in a design, but the route to it is unclear. Can an owner reach it from the starting screen, choose a day, and finish the task? A user flow makes the sequence and decisions visible, including routes that do not end in success.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A user flow maps the steps a user takes to accomplish a task within a product. A flow identifies entry points, actions or screens, decisions, and possible endpoints.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Sketch a flow by naming the user’s task, mapping the steps and decision branches, and marking completion or failure endpoints. Review the flow for missing steps and unnecessary friction between the entry point and the user’s goal.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Sketch an illustrative flow in words: enter from the order home screen, open the closing summary, choose a day, and review the unfinished orders. At the results step, branch on whether any matching orders exist. If there are matches, the owner may open details and return to the summary; if there are none, an empty result ends that route. Mark a failure endpoint for an unavailable result if the example design includes it. Review whether the owner can return from details and whether day selection is actually reachable. These are proposed product steps, not instructions for a real application. The sketch makes missing routes easier to discuss than an isolated picture of the final screen.

teaching_blocks.content: Follow the user's task from entry to endpoint, not only the route a designer hopes users will take. A decision branch requires its possible outcomes to be considered; otherwise the flow may silently omit a case. Remove unnecessary friction where the mapped steps reveal it, while keeping the review focused on accomplishing this task within the product rather than mapping the person's entire working day.

teaching_blocks.title: Success Metrics in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The closing-summary feature ships, and the team reports the number of screens it built. That does not yet quantify whether owners are achieving the intended outcome. A success metric should connect the product change to the result the team wants to judge, with a benchmark, target, and assessment period.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A success metric quantifies whether the intended product outcome is being achieved. A useful target links a specific metric to a measurable, achievable result and time boundary.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Choose metrics that match the goal of the proposed change rather than simply collecting available counts. Record the current benchmark, desired target, and period for judging whether the change succeeded.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the example goal is for more owners to complete a closing order review. Choose the percentage of eligible owners completing that review during a defined week, with an invented current benchmark of 40%. A proposed target might be 50% by the end of the next quarter, subject to the team's assessment that the result is achievable. Record the eligibility and completion definitions alongside the benchmark and target. A count of unrelated page visits is available, but does not automatically answer this goal. The target gives the team a measurable result to assess; it does not establish in advance that the new summary will cause that result or that every available count is relevant.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Keep metric, target, and period distinct. The metric says what is quantified; the target says the desired result; the time boundary says when it will be judged. A percentage without its population or a goal without a period leaves the comparison unclear. Choose measures because they match the intended change, rather than rewriting the goal to fit whichever dashboard count is easiest to obtain.

teaching_blocks.title: Product Roadmap in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Your team has several product goals and many possible tasks. Stakeholders need to understand the direction and priorities over time, not inspect every delivery detail. A roadmap provides that directional view, with a planning horizon and level of detail suited to the people using it.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A product roadmap communicates product direction, priorities, and progress over time. Roadmap content and level of detail should be chosen for its audience.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Translate product goals into prioritized initiatives and place them on an understandable planning horizon. Update the roadmap often enough to remain a trustworthy source of direction and progress.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative shop-order roadmap, connect the goal of making unfinished work visible to an early initiative for a closing summary. Put a later initiative for better shared handoffs on the planning horizon if it serves the next prioritized goal. Explain which work is currently progressing and update that information when priorities or progress change. A leadership audience may need goals, initiatives, and the horizon; a delivery team may need a more detailed view relevant to its decisions. Do not crowd the roadmap with every button adjustment or internal task. Those details may exist in delivery work, but including all of them would obscure the direction this particular document is meant to communicate.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Review whether a reader can connect each prioritized initiative to a product goal and understand its place over time. Then check whether the roadmap still reflects current direction and progress. An old view that the team no longer follows is not a trustworthy explanation just because it once represented a plan. Audience-sensitive detail does not mean changing the underlying product facts between audiences.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A roadmap should not be overloaded with all detailed delivery tasks.

teaching_blocks.title: Capacity Planning in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The roadmap asks for more work than the team may be able to complete. Before treating the horizon as feasible, estimate capacity from people, time, and recent completed work. The arithmetic provides a baseline, but changed availability and external constraints still matter.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Capacity planning estimates the work a team can realistically take on with its available people and time. Recent completed work can inform the forecast, but availability and external constraints can change future capacity.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Check planned work against availability, holidays, dependencies, and known risks before committing to a timeframe. Adjust scope or timing when planned work exceeds the capacity available. Calculate historical velocity as completed work units divided by the number of observed iterations; a baseline period forecast is average velocity × available iterations, adjusted for changed availability.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the team completed 48 consistently measured work units across four iterations. Historical average velocity is 48 ÷ 4 = 12 units per iteration. Over three upcoming iterations, the unadjusted baseline is 12 × 3 = 36 units. If the proposed work totals 45 units, it already exceeds that baseline by 9. Now review holidays, changed availability, dependencies, and known risks before deciding what can be committed. If the team chooses an illustrative adjusted forecast of 30 units after that review, a 45-unit plan needs a scope or timing change. The adjusted number is a planning judgment in this example, not a formula that converts each absence into a universally fixed reduction.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Distinguish the historical average, baseline period forecast, and reviewed capacity forecast. Each answers a different part of the planning question. Completed work is useful evidence, but last period's conditions may not hold next period. Adding people also does not guarantee proportional output because coordination overhead can rise. Explain what you changed and why, rather than presenting the largest arithmetic result as a commitment.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Adding people does not guarantee a proportional increase in completed work because coordination overhead can rise.

teaching_blocks.title: Release Planning (Roadmap Sequencing) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The roadmap says the team will improve closing-time visibility, but the team needs to decide which selected work belongs in upcoming release windows. Release planning gives the directional roadmap a more tactical sequence, taking capacity and prerequisites into account rather than assigning every desirable item to the earliest window.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Release planning assigns selected roadmap work to upcoming release windows. A release plan is more tactical and detailed than the roadmap’s directional view.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Group work into release windows by considering goals, priority, scope, capacity, and dependencies. Check that prerequisite work comes early enough to enable dependent items and revise the windows if the schedule is infeasible.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the selected example work includes defining order status, displaying unfinished orders, and opening order details. The display depends on the status information being available. Put prerequisite work in an earlier window or early enough within a feasible window to support the dependent items. Then examine goals, priority, scope, and capacity for each release window. If the first window cannot accommodate both status work and the full display, revise the scope or move dependent work rather than communicating an infeasible sequence. The windows are a proposed plan for this invented product, not a claim that every release must use the same grouping or duration.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Read the release plan in two ways: does it serve the selected product goals, and could the dependency-linked work actually fit its windows? A high priority does not remove the need for an enabling output. Preserve the distinction between the roadmap's directional view and the release plan's more detailed assignments, while keeping both consistent about the intended work.

teaching_blocks.title: Feature Sequencing in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team has already prioritized a closing summary above a smaller status-data change. Yet the summary cannot work until that status information exists. Sequencing takes the prioritized set and turns it into an executable order, explaining dependency-driven adjustments instead of pretending that priority alone makes an item independent.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Feature sequencing places already-prioritized features in an executable order. A feature that requires another feature’s output cannot be scheduled as if it were independent.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: List prerequisites and dependency relationships, then order the features so prerequisites are available when needed. Use the existing relative priorities to choose among feasible sequences and explain any dependency-driven change in order.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative set, let feature A provide the unfinished-status information, B display the closing summary using A, and C improve an independent search view. The prerequisites require A before B. Even if B has the highest relative priority, scheduling B as if A were unnecessary is not feasible. Among executable alternatives, use the existing priorities: if B is more important than C, a sequence of A, B, C may fit the priority rationale better than A, C, B. State that A comes first because it enables B, not because the team silently changed its view of B's value. Confirm that the prerequisite will be available when the dependent feature needs it.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Draw the prerequisite relationships before choosing the order. Then compare only feasible sequences using the existing relative priorities. This keeps two questions separate: which work matters most, and which work must be available first? The example is not a new scoring method. It is a way to make already-prioritized work executable and to explain why the delivered order can differ from the priority list.

teaching_blocks.title: Timeline Estimation in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A stakeholder asks for a delivery date for 60 units of remaining work. A historical completion rate can help forecast the time, but it cannot guarantee that future iterations will repeat the past. Timeline estimation connects work, rate, and calendar assumptions and makes the uncertainty visible.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A delivery forecast connects estimated work with the team’s recent completion rate and available time. With consistently estimated work, estimated iterations equal remaining work units divided by historical average units completed per iteration.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Convert the iteration estimate into a date range using iteration length, current timing, and plausible variation in completion rate. State the forecast’s assumptions about scope, team availability, dependencies, and historical variability.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the team's historical average is 15 consistently estimated units per iteration. The baseline estimate is 60 ÷ 15 = 4 iterations. With two-week iterations and a start at the beginning of the next iteration, that corresponds to eight weeks at the baseline rate. For an illustrative variation check, rates of 12 and 20 units per iteration imply five and three iterations respectively, or ten and six weeks. This gives a six-to-ten-week planning range under those assumed rates. State the current timing, scope, team availability, dependencies, and historical variability used for the forecast. If work starts partway through an iteration, the calendar translation needs to reflect that timing rather than simply labeling four iterations as an exact date.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Keep the unit calculation and date conversion separate. Work divided by rate estimates iterations; iteration length and current timing translate that estimate to the calendar. The range is meaningful only with its assumptions attached. A precise-looking date derived from an average does not eliminate variation, and this example does not establish that every team should use the same range or iteration length.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A historical average is a forecast input, not a guarantee of the same future rate.

teaching_blocks.title: Quarterly Planning in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A team has a longer-term goal of making shop order work more reliable, but needs a coherent plan for the next quarter. Quarterly planning connects that direction to measurable progress over a three-month period, with owners and milestones that fit the available capacity and dependencies.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A quarterly roadmap organizes product direction and intended progress across three-month planning periods. Quarterly goals should connect to longer-term objectives while remaining measurable within the quarter.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Map selected initiatives to goals, assign owners, and identify milestones for the quarter. Check timelines against team capacity and dependencies before communicating the quarterly plan. Review progress and changing conditions to adjust subsequent quarterly priorities.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented quarter, choose a goal of increasing completed closing reviews from 40% to 50% among the intended shop-owner audience. Map the closing-summary initiative to that goal, name its owner, and mark milestones for clarifying behavior, delivering the selected scope, and assessing the agreed measure. Check that enabling status work and team availability support those milestones before communicating the plan. If a dependency moves or capacity changes during the quarter, review progress and the changed conditions when setting subsequent quarterly priorities. “Finish six features” may describe intended activity, but by itself does not state the measurable product outcome this example quarter is meant to advance.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Read across the plan from longer-term objective to quarterly goal, selected initiative, and milestone. The pieces should describe a coherent intended result rather than unrelated work collected under a calendar heading. The three-month boundary helps make the period explicit; it does not make any selected amount of work feasible. Keep capacity and dependencies in the review instead of treating quarter end as a reason to ignore them.

teaching_blocks.title: Initiative Planning in product work
teaching_blocks.content: “Improve order management” is too broad to define a body of work. An initiative gives that strategic direction a specific goal and scope. Its brief makes the intended audience, assumptions, and evidence of success explicit so readers can understand both the outcome sought and the work proposed to advance it.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: An initiative is a body of work intended to advance a specific product or business goal. An initiative brief makes the problem, audience, goal, scope, assumptions, and success criteria explicit.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Start from the strategic theme and describe the outcome the initiative is meant to achieve. Write the included scope, exclusions, and measures that would demonstrate the intended outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the strategic theme is reliable closing-time order work. An illustrative initiative is “Make unfinished paid orders visible at closing.” Its brief names shop owners as the audience and describes overlooked work as the problem. Include the unfinished-order summary and relevant detail access; exclude payment-history redesign and unrelated search enhancements. State the intended result, such as a higher proportion of eligible owners completing a closing review, and record the measure and target the team has agreed. An assumption about existing status information belongs in the brief, where it can be discussed. These boundaries explain why some attractive improvements are not part of this initiative, without asserting that they have no value elsewhere.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Start with what the initiative is meant to achieve, then explain what is included to pursue that outcome. A title alone does not convey scope, and a list of tasks alone does not convey the goal. The success criteria should describe how the intended outcome would be demonstrated, not simply restate that the selected work will be completed.

teaching_blocks.title: Dependency Management (Roadmap-Level) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Your closing summary depends on status information supplied by another team. A date in your own roadmap does not establish when that output will arrive. Dependency management makes the provider, needed output, dependent work, and handoff point visible so the involved teams can review the sequence together.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A dependency exists when one piece of work needs output or information from another. Dependency relationships determine whether tasks can start or finish independently or must be sequenced.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Map dependencies by identifying the provider, needed output, dependent task, and required handoff point. Review dependencies with the involved teams and communicate changes that could delay downstream work.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: In an invented dependency record, the order-data team provides unfinished-status information; the summary team needs it before implementing the result view; the required handoff is before that view begins. Review the output and timing with both teams instead of merely assuming the provider understands your need. If the provider reports a delay, communicate which downstream work could be affected and revisit the sequence with the people involved. A business-function dependency could also matter: a policy decision may be needed before the team can specify which orders count as eligible. That illustrates why dependencies are not limited to engineering work or tasks within a single team.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Ask what a piece of work needs in order to start or finish, who supplies it, and when the handoff is required. Two items appearing in the same month on a roadmap are not necessarily independent. Keep changes connected to their downstream consequences so stakeholders understand what may move and why, rather than reporting only that a provider has missed a date.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Dependencies can cross teams and business functions rather than existing only within one team.
