teaching_blocks.title: Minimum Viable Product (MVP) Scope Definition in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team wants to learn whether a closing summary gives shop owners useful value, but the proposed first version also contains themes, exports, and custom reports. MVP scope asks what must remain for intended users to try the core value and give useful feedback with less initial investment.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: An MVP is a limited product version built to learn whether a product idea meets customer needs with less initial investment. The scope must retain enough of the core value for the intended users to try it and provide useful feedback.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Define the target user and learning goal, then select only the capabilities needed to deliver and test the core value. List excluded enhancements and explain why they are unnecessary for the initial value and learning goal.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative MVP, define the target user as an owner checking unfinished paid orders at closing. The learning goal is whether a simple summary helps that owner identify remaining work. Retain the capability to view the relevant unfinished orders and understand their status. Exclude decorative themes and custom reporting because they are not needed for this initial value and learning goal. Explain those exclusions rather than removing features simply because a shorter list feels more minimal. If the summary omitted the status information required to identify unfinished work, it would no longer preserve the core value being tested. This is a scope argument for this example, not a universal list of features every MVP needs.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Judge each proposed capability against the same target user and learning goal. “Small” is not enough: users must still be able to experience the value the team wants feedback on. Conversely, a useful enhancement may be unnecessary for this first learning step. The definition is not a license to ship an arbitrary incomplete collection of features and call the missing value an experiment.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: An MVP is not simply an arbitrary incomplete product with the maximum number of features removed.

teaching_blocks.title: Value-vs-Effort Matrix in product work
teaching_blocks.content: You need to compare several proposed improvements without treating a large, valuable effort as identical to a small, valuable one. A value-versus-effort matrix makes both dimensions visible. Its quadrants help distinguish strong early candidates from work whose value must be weighed against greater implementation effort.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: An impact-effort matrix compares initiatives on two dimensions: expected value or importance and implementation effort. The four quadrants are high-impact/low-effort, high-impact/high-effort, low-impact/low-effort, and low-impact/high-effort.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Define a common interpretation of impact and effort and plot each initiative in the corresponding quadrant. Use high-impact/low-effort items as strong early candidates and examine the tradeoff for high-impact/high-effort items.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Define impact as contribution to closing-review completion and agree how the team will distinguish high from low effort. In an illustrative set, place a clearer status label in high-impact/low-effort, a major shared-handoff redesign in high-impact/high-effort, a small decorative adjustment in low-impact/low-effort, and an elaborate unused report in low-impact/high-effort. These placements are invented estimates for practicing the matrix, not conclusions about all such features. The status-label change is a strong early candidate under these assumptions. The handoff redesign still deserves examination because high effort does not erase its potential impact. Make the assumed value and effort visible when explaining why each item occupies its quadrant.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: The matrix compares two judgments, so the common meaning of each axis matters. If one item is rated by user value and another by revenue without an agreed interpretation, their positions are hard to compare. Use the quadrants to frame the discussion rather than claiming that a plotted position proves the underlying impact estimate or supplies an exact order for every initiative.

teaching_blocks.title: Impact Assessment in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Two teams both claim their ideas will have “big impact,” but one means more closing reviews and the other means more page visits. Impact assessment needs a common target outcome and scale before those estimates can be compared. It also needs visible evidence and assumptions, not just an enthusiastic label.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Impact assessment estimates how much a proposed initiative would contribute to a target outcome. Choose a common target metric and impact scale before comparing initiatives.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Estimate the expected contribution using research or observed product evidence, then explain the assumptions behind it. State confidence separately so a promising but speculative effect is not treated as equally reliable as an evidence-backed estimate.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Choose closing-review completion as the example target metric. Suppose a status-label improvement is estimated to increase that measure by 5 percentage points based on observed recognition problems, while a reminder is estimated to increase it by 10 points based on a less-tested assumption. Record the estimated contribution and supporting evidence separately from confidence. Under the supplied assumptions, the reminder has the larger expected effect but weaker support; the label change has a smaller, more evidence-backed estimate. Do not combine those descriptions into “the reminder is definitely better.” The numbers are invented predictions that help illustrate the difference between magnitude and reliability, not measured effects already delivered by either proposal.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: First make the comparison about the same outcome and scale. Then ask what product evidence or research supports each contribution and what assumptions bridge the evidence to the estimate. State confidence separately so speculative impact does not masquerade as certainty. A common target makes the estimates comparable; it does not make them true merely because they are expressed numerically.

teaching_blocks.title: RICE Framework in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team needs to compare a change affecting many owners with one that may help fewer owners more strongly. RICE separates reach, impact, confidence, and effort before combining them. The score is useful only when the timeframe, units, and scales are consistent across the initiatives being compared.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: RICE compares initiatives using reach, impact, confidence, and effort. Reach is the estimated number of affected people or occurrences in a specified timeframe.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Impact estimates the contribution per affected person or occurrence to the chosen goal. Confidence expresses how well evidence supports the estimates and is used as a proportional factor. Effort estimates the total work required using a consistent unit such as person-months. Calculate RICE as reach × impact × confidence ÷ effort and compare scores using consistent assumptions and scales.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Use invented inputs for a closing-summary improvement: reach of 1,000 owners in one quarter, impact of 2 on the agreed per-owner scale, confidence of 80%, and effort of 4 person-months. Treat confidence as the proportional factor 0.8. The score is 1,000 × 2 × 0.8 ÷ 4 = 400. A reminder proposal with quarterly reach 800, impact 3 on the same scale, confidence 50%, and effort 2 person-months scores 800 × 3 × 0.5 ÷ 2 = 600. The reminder ranks higher under these assumptions. State what supports each reach and impact estimate, rather than treating the larger score as proof that the predicted benefit will occur.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Inspect the inputs as well as the arithmetic. Reach is a count within the stated period; impact is the estimated contribution per affected person or occurrence; confidence reflects supporting evidence; effort uses one shared work unit. If you entered 80 instead of 0.8 for confidence, this calculation would inflate the score. If the reminder's confidence were revised to 25%, its score would be 300, showing why uncertain inputs matter to the comparison.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A RICE score is not proof that uncertain impact estimates are accurate.

teaching_blocks.title: ICE Framework in product work
teaching_blocks.content: You want a quick comparison of product ideas, but “high impact” alone ignores uncertainty and difficulty. ICE combines impact, confidence, and ease. In the convention used here, higher ease means the work is more straightforward, so it must not be confused with a scale where higher numbers mean more effort.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: ICE compares ideas using impact, confidence, and ease. Impact estimates the expected effect on the target goal.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Confidence rates the certainty that the predicted effect will occur. Ease rates how straightforward the work is to complete, with higher ease favoring less difficult work. Using the ProductPlan convention, rate each factor from 1 to 10, multiply impact × confidence × ease, and rank higher scores first.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For invented ideas, rate a status-label improvement as impact 6, confidence 8, and ease 9 on agreed 1-to-10 scales. Its ICE score is 6 × 8 × 9 = 432. Rate a broader reminder idea as impact 9, confidence 4, and ease 5. It scores 9 × 4 × 5 = 180. Under this ProductPlan convention, the status-label idea ranks higher. The larger impact rating of the reminder does not outweigh its lower confidence and ease in this example. If people disagree about what a confidence rating of 8 means, discuss the shared scale definition before interpreting the score as a meaningful comparison.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Keep the three questions separate: how large is the expected effect, how certain is it, and how straightforward is the work? Then multiply the agreed ratings using the named convention. The numbers remain judgments rather than measurements that eliminate subjectivity. Giving everyone the same scale definitions can improve consistency, but cannot guarantee that their assumptions are correct or that they will agree about the evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: ICE inputs remain subjective; shared scale definitions improve consistency but do not eliminate subjectivity.

teaching_blocks.title: Weighted Scoring in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A team wants its prioritization to reflect more than one strategic consideration. Weighted scoring makes the relative importance of those criteria explicit before options are rated. The resulting total is a combination of assumptions and judgments, not a way to avoid discussing what the team values.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Weighted scoring ranks options by combining ratings across criteria with explicit relative importance weights. Criteria should reflect the current strategic benefits and costs relevant to the decision.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Set criteria, define a consistent scoring scale, and assign weights before evaluating the options. Calculate each option’s total by multiplying each criterion score by its weight and summing the weighted contributions. Compare totals while checking how changes in priorities or assumptions would affect the ranking.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: In an invented comparison, use customer benefit with weight 0.6 and implementation ease with weight 0.4. Agree that both use a 1-to-5 scale where higher is favorable. Option A receives benefit 5 and ease 2, giving 5 × 0.6 + 2 × 0.4 = 3.8. Option B receives benefit 3 and ease 5, giving 3 × 0.6 + 5 × 0.4 = 3.8. The tie makes the tradeoff visible rather than resolving it. If priorities change to benefit weight 0.8 and ease weight 0.2, A scores 4.4 and B scores 3.4. These are example criteria and weights, not a prescribed universal set. Choose the criteria to reflect the actual decision's strategic benefits and costs.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Set criteria, scale meanings, and weights before rating the options. Otherwise the scoring can conceal a change in priorities made to favor a preferred option. Review how altered assumptions affect the totals and explain any remaining disagreement. A sum can be arithmetically correct while still depending on contested ratings or weights; the number does not remove that discussion.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Numerical scores do not remove disagreements about the assumptions used to create them.

teaching_blocks.title: Tradeoff Analysis in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team can deliver a smaller closing summary sooner or spend more time building a richer view. Either choice gives up something the other provides. Tradeoff analysis makes those benefits, costs, and opportunity costs explicit, then recommends an option against the stated priorities.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A tradeoff is a choice in which obtaining one benefit can require accepting a cost or giving up another benefit. Compare alternatives against the same goals, benefits, costs, and constraints.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write the advantages and disadvantages of each option and make the opportunity cost of choosing one explicit. Recommend the option that best fits the stated priorities and explain the downside being accepted.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose option A delivers a basic unfinished-order view within the example's available capacity, while option B adds shared handoff details but needs a longer window. Compare both against the same goal of helping owners identify remaining work, the same timing constraint, and the same available effort. A offers earlier basic value but gives up the richer handoff capability for now. B offers that capability but gives up the earlier delivery of the basic view. If the stated priority is near-term closing visibility, recommend A and explicitly name the accepted downside: staff handoffs remain less well supported initially. If the priority instead centers on shared handoffs, explain why B may fit better under its timing cost.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Do not describe the chosen option only through its advantages and the rejected option only through its faults. A useful recommendation states what is being gained, what is being given up, and why that exchange fits the priorities. The opportunity cost is part of the decision explanation, not an embarrassing detail to omit once an option has been selected.

teaching_blocks.title: Kano Model in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A feature can matter differently depending on whether customers expect it, benefit from better performance, or are pleasantly surprised by it. Kano examines satisfaction associated with presence and absence, not simply whether a feature receives a positive reaction when shown.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Kano classifies features according to how their presence or absence affects customer satisfaction. Basic features are expected and can create dissatisfaction when missing or inadequate.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Performance features increase satisfaction as their performance improves. Delighters can create disproportionate satisfaction when present even though customers may not miss them when absent. Indifferent features attract little customer interest, while dissatisfaction features can upset customers. Classify candidate features using customer feedback and consider the investment needed to provide an appropriate mix.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Use an invented shop-order feedback set. Customers expect order records to be available and become dissatisfied when they are missing; classify that capability as basic under this feedback. Customers report greater satisfaction as finding an order gets faster; classify search performance as a performance feature. A thoughtful closing summary surprises some owners positively, while its absence was not previously a concern; that may support a delighter classification. Feedback showing little interest in a decorative theme may place it in the indifferent category, while an intrusive interruption that upsets customers may belong among dissatisfaction features. These classifications depend on the example feedback, not on the feature names alone. Consider the required investment when choosing an appropriate mix.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: For each candidate, ask what the supplied customer evidence says about both having it and lacking it. Missing a basic expectation and missing a possible delighter are not the same satisfaction problem. Do not label your own favorite feature a delighter just because you are excited by it, or infer a universal classification from this illustrative set of responses.

teaching_blocks.title: Now-Next-Later Framework in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Stakeholders need to understand current and future priorities, but the team does not have enough certainty to promise exact dates for every idea. Now-Next-Later uses coarse priority horizons to communicate that distinction. More distant work can remain visible without being presented as a fixed delivery commitment.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A Now-Next-Later roadmap groups work into current, upcoming, and more distant priorities instead of relying on exact delivery dates. Now describes work currently in focus.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Next describes the work expected to follow the current priorities. Later holds longer-term ideas whose details and timing are less certain. Place initiatives into the three buckets according to priority and readiness, then revisit the buckets as information changes.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented roadmap, place the closing summary in Now because it is currently in focus. Put a shared-handoff improvement in Next because it is expected to follow the current priorities. Place custom reporting in Later because its details and timing are less certain. Explain the priority and readiness assumptions behind the placement. If new information changes what is ready or important, revisit the buckets rather than leaving the old ordering as an unexplained commitment. A stakeholder asking “Is Next guaranteed for next month?” needs the distinction made explicit: this bucket describes upcoming priority, not a fixed completion date. The example order is conditional on the information used to build this roadmap.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Read the labels as different levels of focus and certainty, not hidden calendar dates. Now says what is in focus; Next says what is expected to follow; Later keeps longer-term ideas with less-certain detail and timing. The framework does not remove the need to explain priorities. It changes how the horizon is expressed so uncertain future work need not be given a false precision.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Next and Later are not promises of fixed completion dates.

teaching_blocks.title: MoSCoW Method in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A release has limited scope, and several stakeholders call their preferred additions essential. MoSCoW asks about the consequence of leaving each requirement out of this specific release or timebox. The categories help distinguish non-negotiable needs from important or desirable additions that can wait.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: MoSCoW sorts work into Must-have, Should-have, Could-have, and Won’t-have-for-now categories. Must-haves are non-negotiable requirements for the specified release or timebox.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Should-haves are important but can be deferred without making the current release unusable. Could-haves are desirable additions whose omission has less effect than omitting a Should-have. Won’t-have-for-now items are explicitly outside the current timebox but may be considered later. Agree on the timebox, goals, and category meanings, then classify each requirement by the consequence of leaving it out.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented closing-summary release, agree that showing the relevant unfinished orders is a Must-have because the release cannot serve its specified purpose without it. A useful sorting option could be a Should-have if important but deferrable without making this release unusable. A decorative preference could be a Could-have if omission has less effect. Put custom reporting in Won't-have-for-now if it is explicitly outside this timebox. Discuss these consequences with stakeholders after agreeing on the goals and category meanings; do not assign categories purely from who asks most strongly. The same capability might be categorized differently in a release with a different goal, so keep the example's boundary visible.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Must, Should, Could, and Won't-for-now describe scope importance for the stated timebox. Won't-for-now does not say the idea will never matter. Nor do identical labels establish an objective ranking between items within one category. The classification is useful when people can explain what the release loses if the requirement is absent, rather than using every category as another word for “important.”

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: MoSCoW labels do not supply an objective ranking among all items within the same category.

teaching_blocks.title: Stakeholder Management in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A product decision affects a sponsor, support staff, and shop owners in different ways. Sending identical updates to everyone may not match their needs or influence. Stakeholder analysis identifies those differences and uses them to choose a proportionate engagement approach.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Stakeholder analysis identifies people affected by a product decision and examines their needs and influence. A power-interest map distinguishes high-power/high-interest, high-power/low-interest, low-power/high-interest, and low-power/low-interest stakeholders.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Manage high-power/high-interest stakeholders closely and keep high-power/low-interest stakeholders satisfied. Keep low-power/high-interest stakeholders informed and monitor low-power/low-interest stakeholders with proportionate effort. Create a stakeholder map by listing stakeholders, assessing their power and interest, and choosing the corresponding engagement approach. Use stakeholder analysis to decide whom to engage and tailor the frequency and content of communication.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: In an invented map, assess the initiative sponsor as high power and high interest, a senior budget approver as high power and lower interest, support representatives as lower power and high interest, and a lightly affected observer as lower power and lower interest. Manage the sponsor closely, keep the approver satisfied, keep support informed, and monitor the observer with proportionate effort. These placements are example assessments, not rules about those job titles. List the people's actual needs and influence before mapping them. Use the map to tailor what they receive and how often, such as a decision discussion for the sponsor and relevant preparation updates for support.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: The four combinations distinguish power from interest. Someone can care deeply while having limited influence, or have substantial influence without following every detail. Assess both instead of treating seniority as a complete stakeholder analysis. An engagement plan should follow from that assessment and the information people need, not simply reproduce an unchanged mailing list for every initiative.

teaching_blocks.title: Cross-Functional Collaboration in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Engineering, design, sales, and support attend a meeting about the closing summary, but leave with different expectations. Bringing functions together is only the start. Cross-functional collaboration needs a shared outcome, clear contributions and handoffs, and ways to surface issues across those boundaries.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Cross-functional collaboration brings different specialties together around a shared outcome. A shared goal, clear roles, and open communication help coordinate work across functions.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Map the needed contributions, assign owners, and identify handoffs and shared milestones. Agree on communication channels and review points so issues are surfaced across team boundaries. For cross-functional friction, make each function’s needs and constraints explicit and seek an option that supports the shared outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented initiative, agree that the shared outcome is helping owners identify unfinished work at closing. Map design's contribution to proposed behavior, engineering's contribution to implementing the agreed scope, and customer-facing teams' contribution to explaining and supporting the change. Assign owners for the necessary handoffs and shared milestones, then agree where updates and questions will be exchanged. If sales wants broader scope while engineering raises a capacity constraint, make both needs explicit. Compare an option that preserves the core outcome now and addresses additional needs later, rather than treating either function's preference as the whole goal. The exact contributions and checkpoints should be agreed for the actual partnership.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Follow the work across functions: who supplies what, who receives it, and what shared result the contribution serves. A room full of different specialties does not itself establish those agreements. When friction appears, return to the explicit needs and constraints and seek an option supporting the shared outcome, rather than assuming attendance proves everyone has the same plan.

teaching_blocks.content: Putting people from different functions in one meeting does not by itself establish a shared way of working.

teaching_blocks.title: Consensus Building in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A group says it wants consensus on release scope, but some participants mean unanimous enthusiasm and others mean no unresolved meaningful objection. Without an agreed decision rule, the same discussion can look settled to one person and unfinished to another. Consensus building begins by making that rule explicit.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Consensus building involves developing shared understanding and working toward an agreement people can support. Unanimity requires active support from everyone involved; consent requires no meaningful unresolved objection.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Choose and state the decision rule before the discussion so participants understand how agreement will be established. Invite concerns, investigate their reasons, and revise the proposal or compare alternatives to seek an acceptable agreement. If consensus is impractical, agree on an alternative decision rule explicitly and document the decision and remaining objections.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative scope discussion, the group chooses consent: no meaningful unresolved objection. A support representative raises a concern that the proposed scope leaves common customer questions unanswered. Investigate the reason and revise the proposal or compare alternatives rather than treating the concern as obstruction. Ask participants to state remaining concerns explicitly. If consensus proves impractical, agree on an alternative rule, such as a named decision-maker deciding after input, and record the decision and remaining objections. Do not quietly switch rules while continuing to claim consensus. If the chosen rule had been unanimity, active support from everyone would be required, which differs from the consent rule in this example.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Separate agreement about the decision process from agreement about the proposal. Both matter. Silence does not reliably demonstrate consent, and pressure-induced agreement is not reliable evidence either. The record should show how the decision was established and what concerns remained, rather than converting the absence of spoken resistance into a claim of universal support.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Silence or pressure-induced agreement is not reliable evidence of consent.

teaching_blocks.title: Audience Adaptation in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A single product update must reach leadership, engineering, and support. The facts remain the same, but the recipients need different information to act. Audience adaptation changes emphasis, terminology, and detail without creating incompatible versions of what happened.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Audience adaptation changes emphasis, terminology, and detail to suit the recipient’s needs. Different audiences need different information from the same product update.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Identify what each audience needs to understand or decide, then tailor the message’s content and language accordingly. Keep the underlying facts consistent while varying detail and tone for each audience.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the invented update is that the closing-summary release moved by two weeks because enabling status work is not ready. Leadership may need the effect on the product goal and a decision about timing. Engineering may need the precise dependent scope and handoff issue. Support may need the revised preparation timing and what to tell customers. All three messages should preserve the same delay and reason. Do not tell leadership that delivery is on schedule while telling engineering that it has slipped merely because the audiences differ. Tailor the amount of detail and vocabulary to each recipient's need to understand or decide, rather than copying every technical note into every message.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Ask what the recipient must do with the information, then select the relevant content and language. Adaptation is not selective truth. If two readers compare messages, the underlying facts should agree even when the headings, emphasis, and tone differ. This example keeps the same change visible while explaining different consequences for each audience.

teaching_blocks.title: Status Reporting in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Stakeholders ask whether the initiative is progressing, but the latest update only says the team is busy. A status report compares actual progress with the plan and makes important deviations, blockers, next actions, and help requests understandable for a defined audience.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A status report summarizes current progress, obstacles, risks, and next steps for a defined audience. Compare actual progress with the intended plan and identify significant deviations.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write the update with completed progress, current status, important risks or blockers, and next actions with owners. Make any needed decision or help request explicit and keep the update concise enough for its audience.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented report, write that status definitions are complete, the summary view is in progress, and the planned detail-access work has not started because a needed output is late. Explain the relevant deviation from the intended plan. Name the next action and owner: the dependency owner will confirm a revised handoff, and the product owner will review the affected scope. If a decision is needed about moving the release window, state the request explicitly instead of burying it in a long activity list. Keep the report concise enough for its audience while retaining the obstacle and its consequence. Do not describe unfinished work as complete merely because effort has been spent on it.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: A useful report distinguishes completed progress, current status, risks or blockers, and next steps. Those categories let the reader see both what has happened and what must happen next. The comparison with the plan makes a deviation meaningful; the owner and explicit request make the update actionable rather than simply announcing that there is a problem.

teaching_blocks.title: Executive & Leadership Communication in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Leadership has limited need for the full delivery discussion but needs to make a consequential timing choice. Executive communication places the headline, requested decision or support, and business implication first. Detailed work remains available in a subordinate role rather than hiding the reason for the message.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Executive communication emphasizes the information leadership needs for direction or a decision. Summarize detailed work in terms of business outcomes, progress, and consequential risks.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: First specify the objective of the update: approval asks leadership to authorize a proposed action; strategic buy-in asks for support for the proposed strategic approach; strategic direction asks leadership to guide which strategic course to pursue. Put that decision or ask at the start, then provide supporting detail. Lead with the headline and name the key risk or implication. Keep technical detail subordinate to the executive’s immediate information need.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative update, lead with: “Please approve moving the closing-summary release by two weeks.” This update seeks approval for a specific timing change, not strategic buy-in for the product approach or strategic direction about which course to pursue. Follow with the implication for the intended closing-review outcome, the progress already made, and the key risk: the required status output is not yet available. State the proposed choice and its accepted downside in terms leadership can use to decide. If technical details explain that risk, include only those needed for the immediate question, leaving the longer implementation discussion secondary. This is not a request to omit an important fact. The example makes the same scope and timing problem clear while foregrounding the information relevant to leadership's decision.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Start by identifying the decision or direction needed, not by summarizing every meeting in chronological order. Then connect the headline to business outcomes, progress, and consequential risks. A concise message can still be complete for its purpose when the requested action and key implication are explicit; a long message can remain unhelpful if the ask is hard to find.

teaching_blocks.title: Product Messaging in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A feature announcement says “New status aggregation interface,” but the target shop owner does not know why it matters. Product messaging translates product value into audience-understandable language and connects the problem to a benefit and meaningful differentiation.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Product messaging communicates the product’s value to its intended audience. A clear headline should foreground the customer benefit rather than an unexplained feature label.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write a headline and supporting points that connect the customer problem to the benefit and meaningful differentiation. Check that the language and claims match the chosen audience and positioning.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented closing-summary feature, try the headline “See what still needs finishing before you close.” Supporting points could explain that unfinished orders are gathered in one view and individual details remain accessible. Connect those points to the owner's difficulty reconciling scattered notes. Check the wording against the chosen positioning: if the product is presented as a simple daily order tool, unexplained technical labels do not help that audience understand the benefit. Do not add a claim such as “cuts closing time in half” unless the allowed evidence supports it. The example headline communicates the intended value without pretending that a particular measured result has already been demonstrated.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Read the message from the target customer's perspective. Can they connect the product capability to their problem and a benefit they understand? Meaningful differentiation should match the chosen positioning rather than appear as an unsupported superlative. A headline is not merely a shorter feature label; it should foreground the value, with supporting points that explain what the product offers.

teaching_blocks.title: Roadmap Communication in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A stakeholder sees a roadmap item move and assumes the team has abandoned the goal. Roadmap communication explains direction, priorities, progress, and reasons for change, with detail chosen for the audience. Showing the roadmap alone may leave the important interpretation unstated.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Effective roadmap communication explains the product direction and the reasons behind priorities. The audience determines the appropriate level of detail and emphasis.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Prepare an update that connects priorities and progress to product goals, flags changes, and states what input is needed. Provide a clear way for stakeholders to ask questions and access the current roadmap.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: In an illustrative update, explain that improving closing-time visibility remains the goal, but the summary initiative has moved because enabling status work is later than expected. State what progress is complete, what priority or timing changed, and what input is needed. A sponsor may need the tradeoff and decision request; the delivery team may need the relevant handoff detail. Provide a clear place for questions and access to the current roadmap so readers can follow up rather than relying on a stale attachment. Avoid loading the message with every delivery task when those details make it harder for this audience to understand the direction.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Connect the item-level change back to the product goal and explain the reason behind the priority. Audience-sensitive communication should improve understanding, not create different facts about the roadmap. The current view and a clear question route let stakeholders inspect what you have communicated and raise concerns about the intended direction or its implications.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Providing excessive roadmap detail can make the message harder to understand rather than more useful.

teaching_blocks.title: Conflict Resolution in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Sales wants a broader release and engineering wants to reduce scope. Repeating those positions more forcefully is not yet conflict resolution. The work is to identify the competing needs beneath the disagreement, separate events from blame, and agree on an option with its tradeoff and follow-up explicit.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Conflict resolution identifies and addresses the competing needs beneath disagreement. Listen to each participant’s perspective and separate observable events from blame or interpretation.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Restate the shared goal and underlying needs, then generate alternatives that could address them. Agree on a workable option and state the tradeoff, accepted downside, and follow-up action.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: In an invented discussion, ask sales what customer need the additional scope addresses and engineering what constraint makes it difficult. Restate the shared goal of delivering useful closing-time visibility. Separate “the extra work does not fit the current capacity estimate” from “engineering does not care about customers.” Compare alternatives such as a narrower initial release, a later broader release, or another scope split that supports the shared goal. If the group chooses the narrower version, record the accepted downside for sales and the next action for clarifying how the remaining need will be addressed. The resolution should name the exchange being made, not pretend that every participant's original preference was satisfied.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Listening makes the needs discussable; separating observations from blame makes the disagreement more precise; alternatives give the group choices beyond repeating the initial positions. End with a workable option, tradeoff, and follow-up. A decision without those details may leave participants with incompatible assumptions about what they have accepted.

teaching_blocks.title: Negotiation in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A stakeholder asks for custom reporting in the next release, while the team needs to preserve a feasible closing-summary scope. Negotiation explores why each request matters and seeks a workable agreement. The stated request is a position; the need beneath it may admit more than one response.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Negotiation seeks a workable agreement between people with differing needs or concerns. A stated position is what someone asks for; the underlying need explains why it matters.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Ask about the other party’s concerns, explain your own needs, and look for options that can address both. Compare alternatives and tradeoffs against shared goals rather than treating the conversation as a contest to win.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: In an invented conversation, the stakeholder's position is “Include custom reports now.” Ask what concern drives it. Suppose they need to explain unfinished work to shop owners during a customer meeting. Explain your own need to keep the current release within its available capacity. Compare options against the shared product goal: a simple existing summary for the meeting, a later reporting improvement, or a smaller reporting capability if feasible. Name what each option gives up. Do not offer an arbitrary halfway feature merely to sound balanced; it could leave the meeting need or the scope constraint unresolved. The agreement should address the underlying concerns as far as the chosen option allows.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Distinguish what someone asks for from why they need it. That separation expands the alternatives without dismissing the request. Explain your own needs just as clearly, then compare options and tradeoffs instead of treating the conversation as a contest to win. A forced compromise may settle the words while leaving the underlying conflict intact.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A forced compromise can leave the underlying conflict unresolved.

teaching_blocks.title: Product Backlog Management in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A backlog contains old requests, duplicates in meaning, and unclear future work alongside urgent product needs. An ordered list is useful only when its relevant items and value can be understood. Backlog management reviews that evolving work against the product goal and keeps the upcoming order explainable.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: The product backlog is an ordered, evolving list of work needed to improve the product. The Product Owner is accountable for ordering backlog items and making the backlog visible and understood.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Review a messy backlog against the product goal, remove obsolete items, clarify relevant work, and place the most valuable upcoming items first. Explain the top items’ value and ordering, and revisit the order as customer or business needs change.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative cleanup, inspect requests related to closing-time order visibility. Remove an obsolete request that no longer fits the product, clarify an ambiguous “improve status” item into understandable relevant work, and place valuable upcoming items in order against the current goal. Explain why the closing summary is above an unrelated enhancement, then revisit that ordering when customer or business needs change. In Scrum, the Product Owner is accountable for ordering and making the backlog visible and understood. A PM should not assume that the job title alone overrides that accountability. Items remaining lower in the backlog are possible future work, not a fixed promise that every historical request will be implemented.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: A clean appearance is not enough. Readers need to understand the top items' value and why their order fits the product goal. Keep the list evolving as needs change instead of preserving irrelevant work because someone once added it. The useful outcome is a visible, understandable ordered backlog, not merely fewer lines in a document.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A backlog is not a fixed promise to implement every item ever added to it.

teaching_blocks.title: Effort Estimation in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team disagrees about how much effort an order-summary item represents. One person sees a familiar view; another sees uncertain status behavior. Relative estimation makes those differences discussable by comparing the work with understood items rather than treating story points as a universal clock.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Estimation expresses the anticipated effort, complexity, and uncertainty of work. Story points are relative units rather than a universal conversion into hours.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Compare a work item with previously understood items and discuss differences in effort, risk, and complexity. Planning poker has team members select estimates independently, reveal them, discuss differences, and re-estimate toward agreement. Use estimates to inform scope and planning, then review them against experience to improve future estimates.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: In an invented planning-poker discussion, team members independently choose estimates for the summary item, reveal them together, and discuss why the values differ. A high estimate may reflect uncertainty about status information; a lower one may assume that information is ready. Compare the item with previously understood work and discuss effort, risk, and complexity. Clarify the disputed assumption, then re-estimate toward agreement. Use the resulting estimate to inform scope and planning, and later compare it with experience to improve future estimates. Do not convert a story-point value into the same fixed number of hours for every team, or use the point total as a measure of an individual's productivity.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: The differing estimates are information about the team's understanding, not simply a problem to average away. Relative units let the team compare work within its understood context, while discussion exposes assumptions about uncertainty and complexity. The estimate remains a planning input that can be reviewed against experience rather than a claim of exact effort known in advance.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Story points should not be treated as a measure of an individual’s productivity.

teaching_blocks.title: Technical Feasibility Assessment (PM-Depth) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A proposal promises a closing summary before anyone has checked whether the necessary information and constraints permit it. PM-depth feasibility work brings the intended outcome and product boundaries to engineering, while leaving technical options and implementation design with the people responsible for that evaluation.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Technical feasibility assesses whether a proposed solution can be built with the available technology, skills, and constraints. A PM supplies the intended user outcome and product constraints while engineering evaluates technical options and limitations.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Ask engineering about implementation constraints, dependencies, technical uncertainty, and the effort needed to achieve the proposed behavior. Clarify whether an answer identifies a hard constraint, a manageable risk, or a cost-and-scope tradeoff, then adjust the proposal accordingly. Review a shared specification with engineering: use its proposed behavior and constraints to identify roadblocks, then agree on the features, requirements, and test plans it records. The specification makes the agreed scope and checks explicit rather than leaving the conversation as a list of uncertainties.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative conversation, explain that owners need to identify unfinished paid orders at closing and describe the intended summary behavior. Ask engineering what data or dependencies are required, what is uncertain, and what effort is needed. If an answer says a required status source is unavailable, clarify whether that is a hard constraint, a manageable risk, or a tradeoff requiring changed scope or cost. A narrower behavior may be possible; a missing essential input may require postponing the proposal. Use a shared specification to review this roadblock and agree on the feature, requirements, and test plan. For example, suppose engineering confirms that unfinished paid-order status is available for the selected day but historical status is not. Together specify a selected-day closing summary, require it to show unfinished paid orders for that day, and agree to test it with example orders that are paid and unfinished, paid and finished, and unpaid. Record the expected inclusion of only the paid, unfinished orders and exclude historical summaries from the agreed scope. This is an illustrative agreement, not a claim about a real system. Record the clarified implications and adjust the product proposal accordingly. Do not supply an invented architecture or assume that a PM's confidence replaces engineering's technical evaluation.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Keep the discussion anchored in the outcome the product must support and the constraints it must respect. “Can we build it?” becomes more informative when followed by questions about limitations, uncertainty, dependencies, and effort. Your responsibility in this example is to understand what the answers mean for scope and commitment, not to substitute for implementation design.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A PM-depth feasibility discussion is not a substitute for engineering’s implementation design.

teaching_blocks.title: Sprint Planning (PM/PO Involvement) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team is preparing its next sprint and needs both a clear purpose and feasible selected work. Sprint Planning is collaborative across the Scrum Team. The PM or PO contribution is to clarify product value and scope, not to dictate the Developers' implementation plan.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Sprint Planning creates the upcoming sprint’s plan through collaboration across the Scrum Team. The Product Owner prepares the important backlog items and explains how they map to the Product Goal.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: The team establishes a Sprint Goal, while Developers select feasible work using their past performance and upcoming capacity. Prepare a PM/PO briefing with the proposed goal, priority rationale, clear item scope, and answers to value or requirement questions.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative briefing, propose a goal of making unfinished paid orders visible in the closing view. Prepare the important backlog items, explain their priority in relation to the Product Goal, and be ready to answer value and requirement questions. The team establishes the Sprint Goal, while Developers select feasible work using past performance and upcoming capacity. If detail access does not fit, clarify the value or scope implications instead of demanding that every proposed item be selected. Developers also determine how the selected work becomes a working increment; the product briefing does not turn that technical planning into a PM instruction sheet.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Separate preparing candidate work from selecting the feasible sprint plan. Clear priorities and requirements support the team's planning, but do not erase capacity or the Developers' responsibility for technical work. A useful product contribution gives the team enough understanding to make the selection and discuss its relationship to the goal.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: The PM/PO does not dictate how Developers turn selected backlog items into working product increments.

teaching_blocks.title: Daily Standup (PM/PO Involvement) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: During a Daily Scrum, someone reports that unfinished-status information is blocking selected work. A PM may need to help clarify the product question, but turning the event into a long management update would change its purpose. The event inspects Developer progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapts the upcoming plan.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute Developer event to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the upcoming plan. A Product Owner participates as a Developer when actively working on sprint backlog items; it is not inherently a management status meeting.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Identify impediments or unresolved product questions from the discussion and clarify who needs to act on them. Handle detailed follow-up outside the short event and involve the appropriate owner instead of interrupting team self-management.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: In an illustrative 15-minute event, Developers identify that a status definition remains unresolved. Clarify who needs to act, then arrange a detailed follow-up with the appropriate owner outside the short event. Do not require each Developer to report personal productivity to the PM or interrupt team self-management with an extended requirements debate. A Product Owner participates as a Developer when actively working on sprint backlog items; the event is not inherently a management status meeting. The relevant product follow-up in this example is to resolve the question that impedes work toward the Sprint Goal, not to take control of the Developers' plan.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Keep the impediment visible and the response proportionate to the event's purpose. Identifying a product question and its owner does not require solving every detail inside the 15 minutes. The distinction lets the team inspect and adapt its work while ensuring that a necessary clarification is handled by the right people afterward.

teaching_blocks.title: Sprint Review (PM/PO Involvement) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: At the end of a sprint, stakeholders need to inspect completed product work and discuss what should happen next. A Sprint Review is not just a list of tasks marked finished. It connects what was and was not completed to the goal and product direction, then uses feedback to reconsider upcoming priorities.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A sprint review inspects completed product work with stakeholders and gathers feedback about next steps. The review considers completed and incomplete work in relation to the sprint goal and product direction.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Prepare a review agenda with the goal, demonstrations of completed work, stakeholder questions, and feedback capture. Use feedback and changed circumstances to reconsider upcoming priorities and clarify next steps.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative review, begin with the Sprint Goal of making unfinished paid orders visible. Demonstrate the completed summary behavior, explain that detail access remains incomplete if that is the actual state, and invite stakeholder questions about the value and next steps. Capture feedback, such as a concern about which orders belong in the result, alongside changed circumstances relevant to priorities. Use it to clarify upcoming work rather than assuming the old plan must remain untouched. Keep discussion grounded in the completed work and direction. Examining how the team worked belongs to the retrospective, which is distinct from this inspection of product work with stakeholders.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Prepare the goal, demonstrations, questions, and feedback capture as a coherent review agenda. A demonstration without context may leave stakeholders unsure what result to assess. Feedback without a next-step discussion may remain an unused note. The review should help clarify the product's next direction without misrepresenting incomplete work as completed.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A sprint review is distinct from a retrospective, which examines the team’s working process.

teaching_blocks.title: Sprint Retrospective (PM/PO Involvement) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A retrospective identifies unclear backlog items, a difficult technical handoff, and a recurring team communication problem. The PM cannot simply accept ownership of every action. The event examines how the Scrum Team worked and chooses improvements with ownership appropriate to the issue.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A sprint retrospective inspects how the team worked and plans improvements to quality and effectiveness. The Scrum Team examines interactions, processes, tools, problems, and assumptions and chooses useful improvements.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Triage actions about product goals, backlog clarity, or backlog ordering to the Product Owner’s accountability. Leave technical work planning with Developers and process improvements as collaborative team work rather than automatically assigning every action to the PM/PO. Assign clear follow-up ownership for the chosen improvements and address high-impact changes promptly.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: In an illustrative retrospective, connect an action to clarify product goals and backlog ordering with the Product Owner's accountability. Leave technical work planning with Developers. Treat the communication-process improvement as collaborative team work and agree a clear follow-up owner rather than automatically assigning it to the PM or PO. Discuss interactions, processes, tools, problems, and assumptions to identify useful improvements. Choose high-impact changes for prompt attention and record who will follow through. If the issue is that requirements were repeatedly unclear, describe that process problem and its improvement, rather than using the retrospective only to review the product demonstration again.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: For each action, ask what kind of improvement it is and who is responsible for the corresponding work. Clear ownership does not mean that one role owns every issue discussed. The retrospective's focus is quality and effectiveness of the team's working process, with selected improvements that can be acted on, not merely a collection of complaints without follow-up.

teaching_blocks.title: Backlog Refinement in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Upcoming work says “improve the closing summary,” but the team cannot tell its user outcome, scope, or acceptance conditions. Refinement makes that work clearer and more manageable over time. It may involve several kinds of review rather than one mandatory meeting immediately before execution.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Backlog refinement is ongoing review and clarification of upcoming work so the team can plan and execute it. Refinement can include clarifying requirements, splitting large items, estimating effort, and reconsidering order.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Review an item for a clear user outcome, understood scope, acceptance conditions, dependencies, and manageable size. Work with the team to resolve gaps, split oversized items, and update estimates and ordering as appropriate.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative item, clarify whether the intended outcome is finding unfinished orders or opening their details. Review included scope, acceptance conditions, dependencies, and size with the team. If both outcomes create an oversized item, split it into smaller understandable work where appropriate. Resolve missing status definitions, revisit the estimate after clarification, and reconsider the order against current needs. The result is updated upcoming work the team can better understand and plan. Do not preserve an old estimate when it rests on an assumption the review has just changed, or call an item refined solely because its title has been rewritten neatly.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Refinement checks the substance of the item: what value it serves, what behavior it includes, what conditions matter, and what could prevent it from progressing. Those questions help expose gaps before the work is selected. Keep the process ongoing as understanding evolves rather than treating one scheduled discussion as the only possible time to clarify upcoming work.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Refinement is not limited to a single mandatory meeting held once before execution.

teaching_blocks.title: Technical Debt Management in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Engineering explains that a shortcut in status handling now makes related changes harder. The team must compare addressing that deferred work with delivering new features. Technical debt management makes the current impact and likely future cost visible, instead of dismissing all debt as bad or reserving a universal capacity percentage without justification.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Technical debt is the future cost or reduced flexibility created by development choices that defer technical work. Debt can be taken deliberately or arise inadvertently, and its consequences can accumulate over time.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Identify a debt item by describing the deferred work, its current impact, and the likely cost of leaving it unresolved. Discuss repayment with the team and weigh it against other work using the impact on future delivery and product quality. Reserve an explicit share of available capacity for debt work when its impact justifies it, and explain the resulting feature-versus-debt tradeoff rather than assuming a universal ratio.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented debt item, describe the deferred status-cleanup work, its current effect on changing the closing summary, and the likely cost of leaving it unresolved. Discuss repayment with engineering alongside feature work, considering future delivery and product quality. Suppose the team chooses to reserve 20% of the available capacity for this particular debt because the described impact justifies it. Explain that this reduces capacity for a planned enhancement and name the resulting tradeoff. The 20% is an example decision, not a recommended ratio for every team. The original shortcut may have been a deliberate choice under real constraints or may have arisen inadvertently; either way, inspect its consequences rather than judging only its label.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Debt describes a future cost or reduced flexibility from deferred technical work. Management therefore needs both an account of the debt and a reasoned repayment choice. Do not assume that all feature work must stop whenever debt exists, or that debt can always be ignored. Make the impact, competing work, and accepted capacity tradeoff explicit for this decision.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Technical debt is not inherently a bad decision; some tradeoffs can be reasonable under real constraints.

teaching_blocks.title: Dependency Tracking (Sprint-Level Blockers) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Selected sprint work cannot progress because another team has not supplied the required status output. At this level, the dependency is a blocker to work toward the Sprint Goal. Tracking it means making the needed output, provider, blocked item, and agreed action visible until the problem is resolved.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A sprint-level blocker is a dependency that prevents selected work from progressing toward the Sprint Goal. Identify the needed output, its provider, the blocked item, and the handoff date.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Confirm the provider’s status and coordinate a workaround, alternative sequence, or escalation with the involved teams. Keep the blocker and agreed action visible until the dependency is resolved.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Create an illustrative blocker record naming the status output, the provider team, the closing-summary item that needs it, and the required handoff date. Confirm the provider's actual status. With the teams involved, consider a workaround, a feasible alternative sequence, or escalation when appropriate. Record the agreed next action and keep the blocker visible while the dependency remains unresolved. If the team can work on an independent part first, that is an alternative sequence to coordinate, not proof that the original dependency has disappeared. Update the record when the needed output is available and the blocker is resolved rather than removing it simply because someone has acknowledged the message.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: A blocker description should let a reader connect what is missing to the selected work it prevents. “Waiting on another team” is less informative than the specific output, provider, item, and handoff. Visibility and coordination support the response; they do not substitute for confirming that the required dependency has actually been met.

teaching_blocks.title: Kanban Board Management in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A board shows several order-product cards in review and more waiting to enter that stage. Starting additional review work may feel productive, but a work-in-progress limit sets a boundary on how many items the stage allows. Board management focuses on finishing or unblocking existing work when that boundary is reached.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Workflow states describe the stages a work item passes through from entry to completion. Cards represent individual work items and columns make their current stages visible.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: A WIP limit sets the maximum number of items allowed in a workflow stage. When a stage reaches its limit, help finish or unblock existing items rather than starting additional work in that stage. Review bottlenecks and adjust limits based on observed flow rather than assuming the initial limits are permanent.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Use an illustrative board with Ready, In progress, Review, and Complete columns. Cards represent individual items. If Review has a WIP limit of two and already contains two cards, help finish or unblock those cards rather than adding a third review item. Moving a card should reflect its actual workflow stage, not merely make the board appear less crowded. Observe where flow repeatedly slows and review the limit based on that evidence. These column names and the limit of two are example choices; the concept does not prescribe them for every team. Raising the limit automatically is not necessarily an improvement, since excess parallel work can lengthen delivery time.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Read the board as a visible representation of current work state. The columns describe stages; the cards identify items; the limit constrains the number allowed in a stage. A full column invites attention to existing work and bottlenecks, not a reflex to start more in the same stage. Limits can be adjusted after reviewing observed flow rather than assumed permanent from the first setup.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Higher limits are not automatically better; excess parallel work can lengthen delivery time.

teaching_blocks.title: Definition of Done in product work
teaching_blocks.content: One person calls an increment complete because its main behavior works; another says agreed quality checks remain unfinished. A shared Definition of Done makes the conditions for considering work complete explicit. It is broader than the acceptance conditions describing one particular item's required behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Definition of Done is the team’s shared set of conditions for considering work complete and ready for customers. The conditions should be specific enough for the team to check completion and quality consistently.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Create the definition collaboratively with the people responsible for delivering and using the work. Apply the shared checklist to an increment before treating it as complete, and resolve any unmet conditions.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented team, collaboratively agree a completion checklist with the people responsible for delivering and using the work. Suppose the agreed conditions include checking intended behavior, completing required quality review, and preparing the stipulated customer-facing information. Apply those actual conditions to the increment. If the summary's item-specific criteria are met but the agreed quality review is not, resolve the unmet shared condition before treating the increment as complete. These sample conditions illustrate a team's agreement, not a universal checklist imposed on every product. A specific criterion such as “completed orders do not appear” still belongs to the particular item and is not identical to the whole shared completion definition.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Ask two distinct questions: did this item deliver its required behavior, and did the increment satisfy the team's shared completion conditions? A clear Definition of Done lets people check the latter consistently. Keep conditions specific enough to verify and resolve missing ones rather than changing the meaning of complete depending on who is reporting progress.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Definition of Done is not identical to the item-specific conditions that describe whether a particular requirement was implemented correctly.

teaching_blocks.title: Release Management in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The closing-summary work is technically available, but customer-facing preparation and monitoring still need coordination. Release management links goals and scope to timing, responsibilities, dependencies, and readiness work, while including support for problems that appear after release.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Release management coordinates the tactical and strategic steps involved in preparing a product for launch. Release planning connects agreed scope to delivery timing and responsibilities.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Prepare the plan by defining release goals and scope, sequencing work, and identifying dependencies and readiness tasks. Include post-release monitoring and support so unexpected user problems can be identified and addressed.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative release plan, define the selected summary scope and goal, sequence enabling status work before dependent behavior, and identify owners for delivery and readiness tasks. Include the necessary customer-support preparation and post-release monitoring with clear responsibilities. If unexpected user problems appear, the plan should identify how they can be noticed and addressed. Do not assume that making the software technically available is automatically the same event as a market-facing launch. In this example, availability could precede broader customer introduction while preparation is completed. Those events need coordination, but need not be identical in timing or purpose.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Read the plan from preparation through post-release response. Scope without timing and ownership leaves coordination unclear; delivery timing without readiness and support overlooks part of the release work. Keep the plan focused on the tactical and strategic steps needed for introduction rather than stopping the explanation at “the code is available.”

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Technical availability and a market-facing launch are distinct and need not be the same event.
