teaching_blocks.title: North Star Metrics in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The shop-order product has many dashboard counts, but the team wants a central measure of customer value. A North Star candidate should reflect what customers receive from using the product, remain within the team's influence, and connect to sustained business results rather than simply being the easiest number to display.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A North Star metric captures a central measure of the value customers receive from a product. A useful North Star metric reflects customer value, is within the team’s influence, and is connected to sustained business results.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Choose a candidate by identifying the product’s core customer value and the observable behavior that indicates receipt of that value. Identify contributing input metrics that teams can act on to improve the central value measure.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the example product's core value is helping shops complete their order work reliably. Consider “shops completing their weekly order review” as a candidate observable behavior indicating receipt of that value. Examine whether it actually reflects the stated value, whether the team can influence it, and how it connects to sustained business results. Identify contributing inputs the team can act on, such as reaching the review and completing it, if those fit the chosen definition. A revenue total may be relevant to the business, but revenue alone may not represent whether customers receive this core value. The candidate requires judgment against those conditions; this example does not establish it as the right North Star for every order product.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Start with the value, then choose the behavior that could indicate customers are receiving it. Do not reverse the process by selecting a convenient count and declaring it central. Contributing input metrics should help teams act on the central measure while preserving the distinction between customer value and an unrelated increase in activity.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Revenue alone may not represent whether customers are receiving the product’s core value.

teaching_blocks.title: Objectives and Key Results (OKRs) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A team promises to ship a summary, write documentation, and hold a meeting, then calls the list an OKR. Those are activities, but an OKR pairs a desired direction with measured results. The key results should make achievement of the objective assessable rather than just record that work was done.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: An OKR pairs an objective describing a desired direction with key results that measure its achievement. The objective is qualitative and motivating; key results are measurable outcomes with clear targets.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write an OKR by stating the intended improvement and a small set of measurable results that would demonstrate it. Review progress against the key-result targets during the agreed planning period.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented OKR, write the objective “Make closing-time order work more reliable for shop owners.” Pair it with a small set of measurable outcomes, such as increasing weekly review completion from 40% to 50% and reducing the defined rate of overlooked unfinished orders from 10% to 5% during the agreed quarter. These are illustrative targets, not product performance claims. Review progress against them during that planning period. Delivering the summary may be an activity intended to contribute, but completing it does not by itself demonstrate that either key result was achieved. Keep the qualitative objective and quantitative outcome targets distinct.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Read each proposed key result and ask whether it measures achievement or merely names something the team will do. The objective communicates direction; the key results define observable success. If the team finishes every activity while the outcome measures remain unchanged, the activity list alone cannot establish that the OKR was achieved.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Completing a list of activities does not by itself demonstrate achievement of a key result.

teaching_blocks.title: Leading and Lagging Indicators in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team wants early signals it can act on and later measures showing whether the intended outcome followed. Leading and lagging labels depend on the target outcome being considered. A metric is classified by its relationship to that outcome, not solely by whether its chart appears early in a dashboard.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A leading indicator tracks a precursor that can help predict a later outcome. A lagging indicator measures an outcome after it has occurred.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Classify a metric by asking whether it measures an input or precursor to the target outcome or the realized outcome itself. Use leading indicators to guide timely action and lagging indicators to check whether the intended result followed.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative target of completing a closing review, opening the review may be a precursor and thus a leading candidate, while completed reviews measure the realized outcome and are lagging relative to that target. If the target becomes sustained weekly use, a completed first review could itself be an earlier precursor. State the target each time you classify the metric. Use the precursor to guide timely investigation or action, then inspect the realized outcome to see whether the intended result followed. More openings do not guarantee more completions; a leading indicator can help predict an outcome without making it inevitable.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Ask whether the measure records an input or precursor to the specified outcome, or the outcome after it occurs. Then explain how the team will use each. The distinction helps connect early action to later checking, but does not establish a causal relationship or guarantee from the label alone.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A leading indicator is not a guarantee of the later outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: Hypothesis Testing in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team expects clearer status labels to improve closing reviews, but “users will love it” is too vague to test. A product hypothesis specifies a change, audience, expected metric direction, and conditions under which the expectation could succeed or be contradicted by evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A hypothesis states an expectation that can be evaluated using evidence. A testable product hypothesis links a specific proposed change to an expected outcome for a defined audience.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write the hypothesis by specifying the change, expected metric direction, affected audience, and conditions for judging the result. Check that the expectation can be contradicted by an observable result rather than merely expressing an aspiration. Set the smallest result that would count as success and identify evidence that would contradict the expectation before testing it.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented hypothesis, write: “For eligible shop owners using the closing summary, clearer status labels will increase weekly review completion by at least 5 percentage points during the planned observation period.” Specify the baseline and the agreed measurement conditions before testing. Define the smallest result that counts as success and what evidence would contradict the expectation, such as no increase or a decrease under those conditions. If the result is a smaller increase, it does not meet the example's specified 5-point success boundary. The hypothesis is an expectation to evaluate, not a statement that the labels already produce that effect or a requirement to reinterpret every favorable result as success.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Make the expectation specific enough that an observable outcome can challenge it. The audience and conditions keep the comparison meaningful, while the success boundary prevents the team from selecting a new definition of success after seeing the result. An aspiration without a possible contradictory observation is not yet a testable product hypothesis.

teaching_blocks.title: Analytics Dashboard Interpretation in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A dashboard shows closing reviews rising sharply this week. The team immediately attributes the change to a new summary. Dashboard interpretation first establishes what the metric and chart actually show, then separates that observation from possible explanations requiring further evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A product analytics dashboard brings together measures that support monitoring product performance. Interpret a chart in the context of its metric definition, time window, audience, and benchmark or target.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Look for changes in trend or unusual values and compare related measures before drawing a conclusion. State the observed anomaly separately from a plausible explanation and identify what further evidence would test that explanation.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: In an illustrative dashboard, completed reviews rise from 400 to 600 in a week, while eligible active shops also rise from 800 to 1,200. The completion proportion remains 50% in both periods. Review the metric definitions, time windows, audience, and benchmark before concluding that owners are completing reviews at a higher rate. State the observed increase in counts separately from an explanation such as newly acquired users or a product change. Identify further evidence that would test the proposed explanation. The supplied arithmetic describes these invented counts; it does not establish why the population grew or why individual customers behaved as they did.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Related measures can change how an apparent anomaly is interpreted. A rise in a total and a rise in the proportion achieving an outcome are different observations. Keep the chart reading precise, and keep explanations labeled as explanations to investigate. A dashboard correlation alone does not establish the cause of a change.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A dashboard correlation alone does not establish why a metric changed.

teaching_blocks.title: Measurement Plan Definition in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team wants to assess whether shop owners complete closing reviews, but has not agreed what data records completion. A measurement plan begins with the product question and defines the key events and contextual properties needed to answer it consistently.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: An event records a user action or occurrence in a product, and event properties describe its context. A tracking plan defines the events and properties to collect so product questions can be answered consistently.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Start a tracking plan with the questions to answer, then list only the key events needed to answer them. For each event, specify its name, when it occurs, source, owner, and relevant properties with types and expected values. Use consistent naming and review the plan with implementation partners before collecting the data.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative tracking plan, start with “How many eligible owners complete a closing review?” Define an event named Closing Review Completed that occurs when the stipulated completion action happens. In this proposed plan, set the source as the closing-summary completion action and the owner as the product analytics partner. Define review date as text in YYYY-MM-DD form, for example 2026-04-08. If shop category is needed for the question, define it as text with the stipulated values “single-owner” and “shift-team.” These names and values are proposed example definitions, not existing tool behavior. Use consistent naming and review the plan with implementation partners before collection. If opening the review is needed to answer a related question, define that separately rather than silently treating an opening as a completion.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: The event says what happened; its properties describe relevant context. The plan connects those records to the questions they should answer and makes timing, source, ownership, and expected values explicit. Tracking every click is not automatically better: it can add unnecessary data and implementation work without improving understanding of the intended product question.

teaching_blocks.content: Tracking every click can create unnecessary data and implementation work rather than better understanding.

teaching_blocks.title: Funnel Analysis in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A team knows that some owners begin a closing review but fewer finish it. Funnel analysis locates where the loss occurs by defining an ordered sequence and comparing counts between steps. Those counts help identify stages to investigate, but do not by themselves explain the users' reasons.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A funnel is an ordered sequence of actions leading toward a target outcome. Conversion is completion of the target step; drop-off is the loss of users between steps.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Define the steps and timeframe, then compare the number of users reaching each step. Calculate a step’s conversion as users reaching the next step divided by users at the previous step, and use the difference to locate drop-off. Investigate the stages with substantial drop-off to identify friction rather than assuming the counts explain its cause.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Use invented counts within a defined one-week window: 1,000 users open the summary, 600 reach the unfinished-order list, and 300 complete the review. Conversion from opening to the list is 600 ÷ 1,000 = 60%; the count drop-off is 400 users. Conversion from the list to completion is 300 ÷ 600 = 50%; the count drop-off is 300 users. Overall completion from the first step is 300 ÷ 1,000 = 30%. State the steps and timeframe alongside these results so the denominators are clear. Investigate the substantial losses at both stages without claiming the counts prove that a particular button, instruction, or design caused them.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: A step conversion uses the previous step's users as its denominator, not the starting population for every calculation. The corresponding count difference locates loss between those steps. Keep step conversion distinct from overall conversion, then use the mapped losses to choose where to investigate friction. A funnel makes the location of drop-off visible while leaving its cause open to further evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Cohort Analysis in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The overall number of active shops is stable, but that total may combine returning customers and newly acquired ones. Cohort analysis follows a defined group over time so continued use can be examined without hiding it inside an aggregate customer count.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A cohort is a group of users who share a defined characteristic or behavior. Retention analysis follows whether members of a defined cohort return or remain active over time.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Define the cohort entry condition and the action that counts as a return, then observe later periods relative to entry. Compare retention across cohorts or periods to see whether continued use is improving or declining.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Define an illustrative cohort as shops completing their first closing review in week A, and define return as completing another review in a later relative week. Suppose 100 shops enter that cohort and 40 complete a review in the first week after entry. Its week-one retention is 40% under that definition. A second cohort entering in week B has 100 shops, with 50 returning in its first week after entry, giving 50%. Compare the same relative period and return action for both. These invented values show a difference in continued use; they do not establish why the cohorts differ. Do not compare the newer cohort's first week with the older cohort's fourth week as if the elapsed periods were equivalent.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Make entry condition, return action, and time since entry explicit. A cohort is defined by a shared characteristic or behavior, not merely any collection of users selected after seeing a favorable result. Following the group through later periods helps distinguish continued use from changes in acquisition that an overall active count can obscure.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: An overall customer count can obscure differences between newly acquired users and established users.

teaching_blocks.title: A/B Testing in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A changed closing-summary version has a higher completion rate than the current version, but a favorable difference alone does not establish improvement. A/B testing compares control and changed experiences under planned conditions, using random assignment and a predefined outcome rather than an informal comparison of whichever users received each version.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A/B testing compares a control experience with a changed version to assess a predefined outcome. Random assignment helps make the comparison less dependent on preexisting differences between user groups.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Define a hypothesis, primary metric, target audience, and planned run conditions before exposing users to the variants. Treat a favorable metric difference as evidence of improvement only when the reported result is statistically significant under the experiment’s chosen threshold—meaning the reported difference meets a preselected statistical standard for distinguishing an effect from random variation; a Not Significant or Inconclusive result does not establish improvement. Duration feasibility depends on available traffic, baseline performance, and the smallest effect the test is intended to detect. Use those inputs to estimate sample needs and duration before building or starting the experiment. In Amplitude’s Duration Estimator, select Estimate Duration. Add a traffic event and conversion success metric, or manually enter total daily traffic and baseline conversion. Set the relative minimum detectable effect (MDE), the smallest proportional improvement you want to detect, and the confidence level. Read the estimated days and users per day. For a plan exposing all that traffic, multiply days by users per day for an approximate total sample; divide by two for an equal two-variant allocation. These are traffic-based estimates derived from the outputs, not a separate sample-size output from the tool.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative experiment, define the hypothesis that clearer status wording improves review completion among eligible shop owners. Specify the primary metric, audience, assignment, and planned run conditions before exposure. Suppose the reported control result is 40% and the changed version is 43%. If the experiment reports Not Significant or Inconclusive under its chosen threshold, that favorable numerical difference does not establish improvement. If the result is statistically significant under that threshold, the favorable difference can be treated as evidence of improvement. These outcomes are illustrative report interpretations, not a significance calculation from the percentages alone. Before building or starting the experiment, use traffic, baseline performance, and the smallest effect to detect to estimate sample needs and duration. For a planning example, select Estimate Duration and manually enter 1,000 total daily users and 40% baseline conversion. Set a 10% relative MDE (a rise from 40% to 44%) and 95% confidence. Suppose the displayed estimate is 20 days and 1,000 users per day. With all that traffic exposed, the approximate total is 20 × 1,000 = 20,000 users, or 10,000 per variant under equal two-variant allocation. The displayed outputs here are stipulated example data, not a calculation predicting what Amplitude will return for those inputs.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Random assignment helps reduce dependence on preexisting group differences, while the planned metric and conditions define what the comparison is meant to assess. Duration feasibility is not a universal number of days: small desired improvements can need more traffic and longer runtimes than larger effects. Keep this PM-level explanation focused on interpreting the reported outcome and planning inputs rather than inventing a statistical formula or claiming that any favorable difference proves success.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Small desired improvements can require more traffic and longer runtimes than larger effects.

teaching_blocks.title: Data-Driven Decision Making in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Evidence suggests one option, but the team also faces customer context and product constraints not captured in the available historical data. Data-informed and data-driven approaches differ in how strongly data determines the choice. In either discussion, explain what the evidence supports and which assumptions or uncertainties shape the recommendation.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Data-informed decision making uses evidence as an input while also considering context and judgment. Data-driven decision making places stronger emphasis on allowing data to determine the choice.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Identify the decision and relevant evidence, interpret what the data supports, and consider qualitative context and constraints. Explain the chosen action in terms of the evidence, assumptions, and uncertainties that shaped it.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose an invented dashboard shows more completed closing reviews after a change, while interviews describe unresolved confusion among shops coordinating shifts. Identify the decision: whether to expand the current summary or address the shift-handoff need. Examine what the quantitative evidence says about the defined audience and outcome, then consider the qualitative context and constraints. A data-informed recommendation uses evidence as an input alongside that judgment. A more data-driven approach places stronger emphasis on letting data determine the choice. If you recommend the handoff improvement, explain the supporting observations and uncertainty instead of saying the current dashboard proves that new direction will work. Historical data may not capture the opportunity or context of the proposed direction.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Begin with the decision, not with whichever chart is available. Interpret the relevant evidence, name what remains unknown, and state how context influenced the action. This makes the recommendation inspectable without treating data as either irrelevant or an all-purpose answer to every product question.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Available historical data may not capture the opportunity or context of a new direction.

teaching_blocks.title: Feature Flags in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team wants to introduce a closing-summary change gradually and retain a way to withdraw it if quality problems appear. A feature flag controls whether specified users receive the feature without requiring a new deployment for every exposure change. The rollout plan still needs audience, checks, and rollback conditions.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A feature flag changes whether specified users receive a feature without requiring a new deployment for each exposure change. Percentage rollout exposes a controlled fraction of eligible users to the feature.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Choose the eligible audience and initial exposure, monitor the result, and expand exposure only after checking readiness. Preserve an explicit rollback option so a problematic change can be turned off or withdrawn. Write explicit exposure stages with a success-metric and feedback check before expanding, and a quality rollback trigger such as errors in the logs that calls for switching the flag off until the problem is fixed.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented staged rollout, define eligible shop owners and begin with 10% exposure. Before expanding to 50% and then 100%, check the agreed completion metric, customer feedback, and readiness at each stage. Record an explicit quality rollback trigger, such as the stipulated error condition appearing in logs, that calls for switching the flag off until the problem is fixed. Those percentages and stages are example choices, not a universal schedule. Preserve the withdrawal option rather than treating expansion as automatic once the calendar advances. If completion improves during exposure, the flag alone does not establish that the change caused the improvement.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Separate deployment from exposure changes, and separate rollout control from causal evidence. The flag lets the team specify who receives the feature and adjust that exposure. Monitoring and readiness checks determine whether the example plan should expand or roll back. Write the stages and triggers explicitly so “gradual rollout” does not hide an undefined sequence or response to problems.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A feature flag by itself does not establish that a change caused an improvement.

teaching_blocks.title: Holdout Groups in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The team wants a comparison baseline that remains excluded while a change is observed over time. A holdout is a subset of users kept out of specified changes. Its usefulness depends on a defined audience, comparison metric, observation period, and consistent assignment and exclusions.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A holdout group is a subset of users excluded from a change so it remains a comparison baseline. Comparing target outcomes for exposed users with the held-out baseline helps estimate the change’s incremental effect over time.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Define the eligible audience, holdout size, excluded changes, comparison metric, and observation period. Choose the holdout size using both available traffic and the statistical needs of the comparison; Amplitude requires choosing a percentage between 1% and 10% when creating the group, not a universal range for every holdout. Withholding more traffic can extend experiment duration, and Amplitude does not allow changing the percentage after creation. Keep assignment and exclusions consistent through the observation period so baseline users do not receive the treatment.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative eligible audience, select a 5% holdout and keep it excluded from the specified closing-summary change throughout the observation period. Compare the defined completion outcome for exposed users with the held-out baseline to help estimate incremental effect over time. Choose the holdout size using traffic and statistical comparison needs, not just because 5% is convenient. In Amplitude, choose this 5% within the allowed 1–10% range at creation; that tool-specific range is not a universal requirement for every holdout. Before creating it, consider whether withholding 5% leaves enough traffic for the planned experiment duration: withholding more traffic can extend that duration. Do not plan to start at 5% and raise it later, because Amplitude prohibits changing the percentage after creation. Also check which experiments were configured to include this holdout. An Amplitude holdout does not protect its users from an experiment that was not configured to include it. The example's exclusion boundary must therefore remain explicit.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: A baseline cannot remain untreated if its members receive the specified treatment during observation. Keep assignment and exclusions consistent rather than moving users between groups to improve a result. The comparison helps estimate the change's incremental effect; the holdout definition, size, exclusions, metric, and period explain what is actually being compared.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A holdout configured in Amplitude cannot protect users from experiments that were not configured to include that holdout.

teaching_blocks.title: Launch Readiness Assessment in product work
teaching_blocks.content: The feature appears ready technically, but support preparation or monitoring may still be incomplete. Launch readiness assesses the capabilities needed to introduce and support the product safely. A recommendation should point to evidence and unmet gates, not rely on a general impression that the team has worked hard.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Launch readiness checks whether the capabilities needed to safely introduce and support the product are in place. Readiness includes technical quality, support preparation, sales preparation, monitoring, and operational response.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Complete each readiness check with evidence, a responsible owner, and an unresolved action for any failed item. Use the agreed checklist to recommend proceeding or holding, explicitly identifying any unmet gate and the risk it creates.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative checklist, assess technical quality, support preparation, sales preparation, monitoring, and operational response. Record evidence and a responsible owner for each check. Suppose the technical-quality owner has recorded completion of the agreed checks, but the monitoring owner has not completed the required alert check. Record monitoring as an unmet gate, assign its owner the action of completing and documenting that check, and identify the risk that unexpected user problems might not be noticed promptly. Recommend holding under this example checklist until the gate is met. Conversely, a proceed recommendation should explain how the agreed gates have been met. Do not turn the sample dimensions into a claim that every launch has exactly the same checklist or that a green technical item makes every other readiness dimension irrelevant.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Link the recommendation to the actual agreed checks. Evidence supports the status; the owner and unresolved action explain how a failed item will be addressed; the risk explains why it matters to the launch decision. A checklist filled with unsupported green labels does not give the same basis for a go/no-go recommendation.

teaching_blocks.title: Launch Communication Planning in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A launch date is agreed, but support hears about the change at the same time as customers and does not know how to answer questions. Launch communication planning specifies who needs which information, through which channel, from which owner, and when before, during, and after introduction.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A communication plan specifies how relevant information will reach the people who need it. The plan identifies audiences, messages, channels, timing, and responsible communicators.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Build a plan by mapping each audience’s information needs to a message, delivery channel, owner, and cadence. Review whether messages are reaching the intended audience and update the plan when project needs change. For a launch, sequence audience-specific messages before, during, and after introduction and specify the owner and channel for each.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented Wednesday launch, schedule a support briefing on Monday, a customer benefit message on Wednesday, and a follow-up update on Friday. Let the support lead own the Monday team briefing, the product communications owner deliver the Wednesday customer email, and the support lead send the Friday follow-up through the agreed customer channel. For each, record the audience's information need, message, channel, timing, and responsible communicator. Support's briefing might explain behavior and limitations; the customer message might explain the benefit and where to find the new summary. Give the post-launch update an owner and channel too, rather than assuming it happens automatically. These are illustrative message choices, not a mandated timing interval. Review whether messages reach the intended audience and revise the plan if project needs or launch timing change.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Sequence communication around introduction while preserving audience-specific needs. A launch date alone does not specify a communication plan, and one general announcement may not supply everyone with usable information. Keeping owner and channel beside each message makes the plan more concrete than a list of audiences with no delivery responsibility.

teaching_blocks.title: Sales & Support Enablement Basics in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Sales and support know a closing-summary feature is arriving, but cannot explain its value or answer common questions unaided. Enablement prepares customer-facing teams with relevant knowledge, training, documentation, and practical materials before broad introduction.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Product enablement prepares customer-facing teams to explain and support a product effectively. Enablement can include product knowledge, training, documentation, and practical materials for sales and support.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Identify each team’s needs and build an enablement plan with materials, training sessions, owners, and completion timing. Check that customer-facing teams can explain the product’s value and handle common questions before broad introduction. Prepare an enablement packet with the feature’s value, talking points, frequently asked questions, known limitations, and an escalation route. Build the FAQ by listing customer questions raised by the feature and recording answers in a support-team reference. For talking points, provide a brief product description, a short positioning statement, and value pillars that explain how the feature delivers value and addresses customer pain points. Build the known-limitations reference from the product requirements, listing specifically what is out of scope for the feature or release; update that list as the requirements evolve.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative enablement packet, include the feature's intended value for shop owners, clear talking points, frequently asked questions, known limitations, and an escalation route. For the stipulated example behavior, include the FAQ “Which orders appear?” with the answer “Unfinished paid orders for the selected day.” Build the talking points around the stipulated behavior. Brief description: “A selected-day summary of unfinished paid orders.” Positioning: “For shop owners reviewing remaining work before closing, this summary brings unfinished paid orders for the selected day into one view.” Value pillars: “Visibility into remaining work—the summary shows unfinished paid orders, addressing the owner’s question about what still needs attention; a focused daily review—the selected-day scope keeps the review on that day’s remaining orders, addressing the difficulty of separating today’s work from other days.” These are intended values, not measured performance claims. Use the product requirements to record the example limitation “This release does not edit payment history,” and name the product support owner as the escalation contact for unresolved questions. For an illustrative requirements update, suppose the agreed requirements are clarified to exclude historical-day summaries from this release. Add “Historical-day summaries are out of scope for this release” to the known-limitations reference and revise the FAQ to specify that the selected day is the current closing day. Keep the payment-history limitation unless the requirements change it. These packet contents must match the actual agreed feature rather than promise unsupported cases. Build the plan around each team's needs, with materials, training sessions, owners, and completion timing. Check whether the teams can explain the value and handle common questions before broad introduction rather than marking enablement complete simply because a document was sent.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Think from the representative's perspective: can this packet support an accurate explanation without needing an engineer to interpret every sentence? Keep claims and limitations consistent with the actual feature. The packet's practical content and the team's preparation work together; neither a slogan without answers nor a detailed document nobody can use fulfills the example need.

teaching_blocks.title: Design Collaboration in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A PM dislikes a proposed layout, while the designer explains that it addresses a documented user difficulty. Design collaboration should examine user needs, goals, constraints, alternatives, and rationale rather than treating personal preference as the shared decision criterion.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Design collaboration combines understanding of user needs with design and technical perspectives. The shared discussion should focus on the user problem and product goals rather than personal preferences.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Prepare a design discussion with the problem, relevant research, goals, and constraints. Invite design alternatives, evaluate them against the shared criteria, and record questions and next steps. The PM contributes the user problem, goals, and product constraints; designers contribute design alternatives and rationale, with review checkpoints agreed across the partnership. Agree who makes each design decision and who contributes advice; when the responsible designer is the agreed decision-maker, contributors supply information and recommendations but leave the final call to that designer.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative review, prepare the closing-time problem, relevant research, product goal, and constraints. The PM explains the intended outcome and product boundaries; the designer presents alternatives and their rationale. Evaluate those alternatives against shared criteria and record unresolved questions and next steps. Agree review checkpoints and who makes each decision. If the responsible designer is the agreed decision-maker for the layout, the PM contributes information and recommendations but leaves the final call to that designer. Do not turn that conditional agreement into a claim that one role universally controls every design decision. A critique of an observable product issue is not an attack on the person who created it.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Make the partnership's contributions and decision authority explicit. Shared discussion does not mean that every contributor has identical authority, and agreed authority does not mean relevant product constraints are ignored. Keep the review focused on the user problem and product goals so disagreement about an alternative can be discussed through evidence and rationale rather than personal taste.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear

teaching_blocks.title: User Journey Mapping in product work
teaching_blocks.content: An owner has difficulty at closing, but the isolated summary screen does not show everything the person goes through to finish the task. A journey map represents the process around a chosen actor and scenario, including actions, thoughts, emotions, and opportunities grounded in research.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: A journey map visualizes the process a person goes through to accomplish a goal. A journey map specifies an actor, scenario, phases, actions, thoughts, emotions, and opportunities.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Choose the actor and scenario, map the phases and actions, and add research-grounded thoughts and emotions. Use the mapped experience to identify pain points and opportunities for improvement.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative actor, choose a shop owner preparing to close. Map phases such as gathering order records, identifying unfinished work, and planning the next day. Add the actions observed or reported in research. If the research supports it, record a thought such as uncertainty about missing paid work and an emotion such as frustration during reconciliation. Use the mapped pain points to identify improvement opportunities. If those thoughts or emotions are only assumptions in an early exercise, label them as assumptions rather than presenting them as research evidence. This journey concerns the person's process of accomplishing the closing goal, not merely the product screens in one user flow.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Keep actor and scenario specific so the phases describe a coherent experience. Research-grounded thoughts and emotions explain parts of that experience that action names alone may miss. The map can reveal where an opportunity relates to a pain point, but its visual completeness does not turn assumed content into evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A journey map should not be presented as research evidence when its contents are only assumptions.

teaching_blocks.title: Giving Design Feedback in product work
teaching_blocks.content: A review comment says “This design feels wrong,” and the designer cannot tell what to change or why. Constructive feedback separates an observable issue from your interpretation, connects it to the intended user outcome, and makes an actionable request that can be discussed.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Constructive design feedback describes an observable issue and relates it to the intended user outcome. Separate an observation from its interpretation so the recipient can understand and discuss the concern.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Give feedback by describing what you observed, explaining its effect or concern, and making a clear, actionable request. Invite the other person’s perspective and discuss whether the requested change addresses the shared goal.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative closing-summary wireframe, say: “The day selector is shown below the results. I am concerned owners may read the list without noticing which day it covers. Could we make the selected day more apparent so the list's context is clear?” The selector's location is the observation; the possible user effect is your interpretation; the request is to make the day more apparent. Invite the designer's perspective and discuss whether the change would address the shared goal. If there is relevant user evidence, distinguish it from your concern instead of implying that your prediction was directly observed. Do not replace the issue with a judgment that the designer was careless or did not understand users.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Review the feedback as three parts: what you observed, why it concerns you in relation to the user outcome, and what you are asking for. The recipient can then understand and challenge the interpretation or suggest another response. An actionable request need not impose your preferred layout when several approaches could address the shared goal.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Judgments about a person’s intentions or character are not the same as observations of their work.

teaching_blocks.title: User Testing Synthesis (Findings to Design Decisions) in product work
teaching_blocks.content: Usability notes describe missed day selection, confusion about status, and one unusual task interruption. Sending the notes to design is not yet synthesis. The work is to interpret reliable observations, distinguish recurring problems from isolated or confounded events, and connect prioritized issues to proposed changes.

teaching_blocks.title: The central idea
teaching_blocks.content: Synthesis connects observed usability problems to design changes rather than merely forwarding session notes. Interpret observations alongside recruitment, task design, facilitation, and other data before treating them as reliable findings.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Look for repeated and consistent evidence and distinguish a real pattern from an isolated or confounded observation. Prioritize usability issues by severity, considering how often each occurs, how difficult it is for users to overcome, and whether it repeatedly bothers them; allocate more effort to the most serious problems. Discuss the proposed changes with design and retain the supporting findings so later decisions can be checked against the original evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Worked Product Manager example
teaching_blocks.content: For an invented finding set, suppose repeated sessions show owners reading results for the wrong day, while one session is interrupted by an unrelated phone call. Interpret the observations alongside recruitment, task design, facilitation, and other data before treating them as reliable findings. For each issue, consider how often it occurs, how difficult it is to overcome, and whether it repeatedly bothers users. If the wrong-day problem is the most serious under those criteria, allocate more effort to it and propose making the selected day more apparent. Discuss the proposal with design and retain the supporting findings so the later decision can be checked against the original evidence. Do not treat the phone interruption as a recurring design problem without appropriate support.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through the example
teaching_blocks.content: Move from recorded observation to supported finding, then from severity judgment to a design recommendation. Keep the evidence available at each step. This lets the team examine both why an issue deserves priority and how the proposed change addresses it, rather than mistaking a long list of session notes for a reasoned design decision.
